_comment_cc ComputeCapability is the CUDA compute capability NVIDIA lists for this part (https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus). A model graph that differs by GPU generation resolves its architecture overlay by the major version, so a chip that states none cannot run such a graph.

b200: provenance notes

_comment B200 SXM. Peak FLOPs and HBM bandwidth are NVIDIA's per-GPU figures for HGX B200 in the NVIDIA Blackwell Datasheet (document 4204213, Oct 2025; https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/01dyp27s6aj4e0483cs5goo15354m438.pdf), table 'Individual Blackwell GPU Specifications': FP4 18 PFLOPS, FP8/FP6 9 PFLOPS, FP16/BF16 4.5 PFLOPS, all stated sparse with the footnote 'Dense is one-half of the sparse spec shown', giving dense FP4 9000, FP8 4500 and BF16 2250 TFLOPS; and '180 GB HBM3E | 7.7 TB/s'. The NVIDIA Blackwell Architecture Technical Brief v2.1 (https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/gl2l4l4812s5fw0p614s6i8bv6mi3vx5.pdf, Table 3) states the same per-GPU rates as dense/sparse pairs (FP4 9/18, FP8 4.5/9, BF16 2.2/4.5 petaFLOPS). AISimulate's system descriptor (https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate/blob/2f0f4cd8606d580567b253d02f3d699fe36db865/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/b200_sxm.yaml) carries the same figures. FP4 has native Tensor-Core support on this part, where on Hopper it is a bandwidth saving only. CAVEAT (memory unit): the datasheet states 180 GB; this entry records it as 180 GiB, the reading AISimulate's descriptor uses (mem_capacity 193273528320 bytes, exactly 180 GiB). The device itself reports 191465652224 bytes (178.3 GiB; NVIDIA's published cudaGetDeviceProperties dump, cited under _comment_sm), which the GiB reading matches within 1% and the decimal reading (167.6 GiB) does not.

_comment_memory MemoryGiB is the device total the CUDA driver reports, which is what vLLM v0.31.0 multiplies by gpu_memory_utilization (requested = ceil(total_memory x gmu), vllm/v1/worker/utils.py:539-558), not the datasheet's 180 GB: 191,503,007,744 B = 178.3511 GiB on 'NVIDIA B200' (PyTorch CUDACachingAllocator 'total: 191503007744' and vLLM start-up logs 'Free memory on device (175.93/178.35 GiB)', driver 580.159.03, InferenceX DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash B200 run, https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/38438383633). NVIDIA's published cudaGetDeviceProperties dump (cited under _comment_sm) reports 191,465,652,224 B (178.32 GiB) on an earlier driver; the serving log is kept because it is the figure the engine sized from. Measured, not vendor_spec; the rest of this file is vendor_spec, and the memory-unit caveat in _comment is superseded by this figure.

_comment_interconnect IntraNodeBwGBps is the NVLink 5 per-GPU unidirectional figure, 900 GB/s: the datasheet's 'Fifth-generation NVLink: 1.8 TB/s' per GPU, bidirectional, halved. A node's GPU count is a property of the deployment rather than of this part, so it comes from the scenario's cluster block; the common chassis is the 8-GPU HGX B200 baseboard. Unlike GB200 this part carries no rack tier: its NVLink domain is the baseboard, so crossing a node boundary is a bandwidth change and the fabric governs. The AISimulate descriptor's reference is CX7 400GbE RoCEv2 at 50 GB/s per GPU; no catalog RoCE fabric matches it (networks/roce-200g.yaml is 25 GB/s), and networks/ib-400g.yaml states the same 50 GB/s over InfiniBand. No GPUsPerRack or IntraRackBwGBps is stated here because there is no rack-wide NVLink domain to describe.

_comment_sm SMCount is the count of ENABLED Streaming Multiprocessors, 148, as NVIDIA publishes it. NVIDIA's datasheet gives no SM count, so the sources are NVIDIA's other publications: the technical blog 'Boost GPU Memory Performance with No Code Changes Using NVIDIA CUDA MPS' (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/boost-gpu-memory-performance-with-no-code-changes-using-nvidia-cuda-mps) describes 'an NVIDIA HGX B200 system with 8 Blackwell GPUs that normally have 148 SMs'; and the device-properties dump NVIDIA publishes in its TensorRT cookbook records multiProcessorCount = 148 for 'NVIDIA B200' (https://github.com/NVIDIA/trt-samples-for-hackathon-cn/blob/fe36094390a4c9293e0ed398dbb29ac336853ffa/cookbook/90-Misc/DeviceInfo/output/b200.txt). It agrees with NVIDIA's Hot Chips 2024 disclosure as reported by chipsandcheese, 74 of 80 SMs enabled on each of two dies (https://chipsandcheese.com/p/nvidias-b200-keeping-the-cuda-juggernaut). The cost model uses SMCount for two things: the per-SM share of peak FLOPs, and the 12-SM derate a Triton-path KV fetch withholds while it overlaps a forward pass (cost model §8.3), which is 8.11% at 148 SMs.

_comment_cc ComputeCapability is the CUDA compute capability NVIDIA lists for this part (https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus). A model graph that differs by GPU generation resolves its architecture overlay by the major version, so a chip that states none cannot run such a graph.

b300: provenance notes

_comment B300 SXM (Blackwell Ultra). Peak FLOPs and HBM bandwidth are NVIDIA's per-GPU figures for HGX B300 in the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra Datasheet (document 4169750, Oct 2025; https://resources.nvidia.com/en-us-blackwell-architecture/blackwell-ultra-datasheet, PDF https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/1k0p832eq8r5ca0u5383ie5o4tp3bst1.pdf), table 'Individual Blackwell Ultra GPU Specifications': FP4 '18 PFLOPS | 14 PFLOPS' (sparse | dense), FP8/FP6 9 PFLOPS and FP16/BF16 4.5 PFLOPS (sparse; 'Dense is ½ sparse spec shown'), giving dense FP4 14000, FP8 4500 and BF16 2250 TFLOPS; and '270 GB HBM3E | 7.7 TB/s'. AISimulate's descriptor (https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate/blob/2f0f4cd8606d580567b253d02f3d699fe36db865/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/b300_sxm.yaml) states the same FLOPs. Its bandwidth differs: it states 7.75 TB/s, computed as the HGX B300 system total of 62 TB/s divided by 8 GPUs. This entry records the datasheet's per-GPU 7.7 TB/s instead. MemoryGiB is NOT a datasheet figure: 268.6 GiB is the capacity nvidia-smi reports (275040 MiB), as the AISimulate descriptor records it (mem_capacity 288400343040 bytes, '275040MiB reported by nvidia-smi'). The datasheet states 270 GB. NVIDIA's published cudaGetDeviceProperties dump for 'NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC' (cited under _comment_sm) reports totalGlobalMem 287428771840 bytes, 267.7 GiB. Two things distinguish this part from B200 and both are recorded because a cost model reads them: dense FP4 is 14000 TFLOPS against B200's 9000, a 1.56x step with no change to the BF16 or FP8 rates; and INT8 drops sharply. The datasheet states INT8 307 TOPS sparse (153.5 dense; the Technical Brief v2.1 Table 3 gives 0.15/0.30 petaOPS) against B200's 9 POPS sparse, and the descriptor's int8_tc_flops of 153.5 TFLOPS matches it. The catalog has no INT8 field, so none is recorded.

_comment_memory MemoryGiB is the device total the CUDA driver reports, which is what vLLM v0.31.0 multiplies by gpu_memory_utilization (requested = ceil(total_memory x gmu), vllm/v1/worker/utils.py:539-558), not nvidia-smi's 275040 MiB (268.6 GiB) or the datasheet's 270 GB: 287,428,771,840 B = 267.6889 GiB on 'NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC' (NVIDIA's published cudaGetDeviceProperties dump, totalGlobalMem, cited under _comment_sm), matching vLLM start-up logs 'Free memory on device (265.24/267.69 GiB)', driver 580.159.03, InferenceX DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash B300 run, https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/38508502533. Measured, not vendor_spec; the rest of this file is vendor_spec, and the MemoryGiB sentence in _comment is superseded by this figure.

_comment_interconnect IntraNodeBwGBps is the NVLink 5 per-GPU unidirectional figure, 900 GB/s: the datasheet's 'Fifth-Generation NVLink: 1.8 TB/s', bidirectional, halved. That is the same as B200. The inter-node fabric differs: the AISimulate descriptor states 100 GB/s per GPU for a 1:1 CX8 XDR 800 Gb/s configuration, double B200's CX7, so a cross-node collective on this part pays half the penalty. That fabric figure lives with the reusable fabric class rather than here: a B300 multi-node scenario names networks/ib-800g.yaml (100 GB/s per GPU). Single-node B300 scenarios are unaffected. Like B200 and unlike GB200 there is no rack-wide NVLink domain, so no rack tier is stated.

_comment_sm SMCount is the count of ENABLED Streaming Multiprocessors, 148, as the device reports it. This is NOT a datasheet figure: no NVIDIA datasheet gives an SM count for this SKU, and NVIDIA's Blackwell Ultra architecture blog states only 160 SMs for the full two-die implementation, with a footnote that available SM count varies by SKU (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/inside-nvidia-blackwell-ultra-the-chip-powering-the-ai-factory-era). The source is the device-properties dump NVIDIA publishes in its TensorRT cookbook, which records multiProcessorCount = 148, compute capability 10.3, for 'NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC' (https://github.com/NVIDIA/trt-samples-for-hackathon-cn/blob/fe36094390a4c9293e0ed398dbb29ac336853ffa/cookbook/90-Misc/DeviceInfo/output/b300.txt). The same dump records 132 for H100 and H200 and 142 for L40S, which matches those parts' datasheets. The cost model uses SMCount for two things: the per-SM share of peak FLOPs, and the 12-SM derate a Triton-path KV fetch withholds while it overlaps a forward pass (cost model §8.3), which is 8.11% at 148 SMs.

_comment_cc ComputeCapability is the CUDA compute capability NVIDIA lists for this part (https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus). A model graph that differs by GPU generation resolves its architecture overlay by the major version, so a chip that states none cannot run such a graph.

gb200-nvl72: provenance notes

_comment GB200 in the NVL72 rack configuration. Peak FLOPs, HBM capacity and HBM bandwidth are NVIDIA's per-GPU figures for GB200 NVL72 in the NVIDIA Blackwell Datasheet (document 4204213, Oct 2025; https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/01dyp27s6aj4e0483cs5goo15354m438.pdf), table 'Individual Blackwell GPU Specifications': FP4 20 PFLOPS, FP8/FP6 10 PFLOPS, FP16/BF16 5 PFLOPS, all stated sparse with the footnote 'Dense is one-half of the sparse spec shown', giving dense FP4 10000, FP8 5000 and BF16 2500 TFLOPS; and '186 GB HBM3E | 8 TB/s'. The rack totals on https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gb200-nvl72/ give the same figures when divided by 72 GPUs (FP4 720 PFLOPS dense, 13.4 TB HBM3E, 576 TB/s). The InferenceX /api/v1/views/gpu-specs record for gb200, this entry's original source (calibration companion §5.2), carries the same figures. Two structural differences from Hopper carry over regardless of the numbers: FP4 has native Tensor-Core support here where on Hopper fp4Tflops is null, confirming FP4 is a bandwidth saving only on that part; and the CPU link is NVLink-C2C rather than PCIe, which changes the offload arithmetic. CAVEAT (memory unit): 186 GB is read here as decimal GB (173.2 GiB), where the H200 entry reads NVIDIA's advertised '141GB' as GiB. The two entries therefore apply different readings of the same kind of figure, because each follows its own original source's units. The readings differ by 7.4%, which matters for capacity planning. For comparison, AISimulate's gb200 descriptor records the capacity nvidia-smi reports, 189471 MiB (185.0 GiB) (https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate/blob/2f0f4cd8606d580567b253d02f3d699fe36db865/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/gb200.yaml).

_comment_memory MemoryGiB is the device total the CUDA driver reports, which is what vLLM v0.31.0 multiplies by gpu_memory_utilization (requested = ceil(total_memory x gmu), vllm/v1/worker/utils.py:539-558), not the datasheet's 186 GB read as decimal (173.2 GiB): vLLM start-up logs 'Free memory on device (180.15/184.0 GiB)' on 'NVIDIA GB200', driver 580.126.20, InferenceX Kimi-K3 GB200 run, https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/38450060269. vLLM prints the total rounded to 0.01 GiB, so this is 184.00 +/- 0.005 GiB; no public log found states the byte count. nvidia-smi's 189471 MiB (185.0 GiB, AISimulate descriptor cited in _comment) includes memory the driver reserves. Measured, not vendor_spec; the rest of this file is vendor_spec, and the memory-unit caveat in _comment is superseded by this figure.

_comment_interconnect This part needs three topology tiers rather than two. The NVL72 rack is built from 18 compute trays (NVIDIA MGX GB200 compute tray: two Grace CPUs and four Blackwell GPUs, each Grace serving two GPUs over NVLink-C2C), joined by an EXTERNAL NVLink switch fabric: nine NVLink switch trays in the same rack carry every GPU's eighteen NVLink 5 links, so any two of the 72 GPUs talk over the switch fabric at the full per-GPU rate (NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 page, https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gb200-nvl72/: '72 Blackwell GPUs ... 36 Grace CPUs', '130 TB/s' NVLink domain, i.e. 72 x 1.8 TB/s). IntraNodeBwGBps is that per-GPU NVLink 5 figure, 900 GB/s: the datasheet's 'Fifth-generation NVLink: 1.8 TB/s', bidirectional, halved. A node here is one tray, so GPUsPerNode is 4, not 8; GPUsPerRack is 72, the 18 trays. IntraRackBwGBps is ALSO 900: inside the rack a tray boundary goes through the same NVLink switches, so crossing it is not a bandwidth change at all. Only the rack boundary is, and it is an 18x step down to InfiniBand (networks/ib-400g.yaml, 50 GB/s nominal per GPU, one ConnectX-7 per GPU). A model keyed on tp > GPUsPerNode alone would wrongly derate this part: the condition is the link, not the chassis count. That 18x step at the rack boundary is what makes EP up to 72 viable within one rack, since at EP=72 no expert traffic leaves it. Since the NVLink domain belongs to the chip rather than to a networks/ fabric, a measured correction to it is scoped by hardware in blis-registry, and a correction to the InfiniBand step by fabric. AISimulate's gb200 descriptor states the same three tiers, and adds inter_rack_latency: 5 µs, annotated '5us typical for InfiniBand between racks'. That is a typical value rather than a vendor specification, and the catalog has no field for it, so this entry does not record it.

_comment_sm SMCount is the count of ENABLED Streaming Multiprocessors per GPU, 152, as the driver reports it on an NVIDIA GB200. This is NOT a datasheet figure and NOT an NVIDIA publication: neither NVIDIA's datasheet nor the InferenceX record gives an SM count for GB200. The source is a device-properties print of one named device: the Triton project's Cluster Launch Control tutorial, whose recorded output reads 'Device: NVIDIA GB200, SMs: 152' from torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0), i.e. cudaDeviceProp.multiProcessorCount (https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/97c02ff4e5025689c596cc668c7c27316bbf64d2/python/tutorials/gluon/12-cluster-launch-control.py#L292, added in triton-lang/triton#9361). FlashInfer's benchmark records agree: its 'Tested versions' table lists 'NVIDIA GB200 | sm_100a | 152 | driver 580.126.20' (https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/cfa0318a1316e8838bdee32c2a2014e22001dabe/flashinfer/experimental/cake/cake_dense_gemm_nondet_train/README.md#L1390), on the driver version this file cites for the MemoryGiB reading. It is not B200's 148 (see hardware/b200.yaml): an earlier version of this entry carried 148 over from B200 on the assumption that the same two dies are enabled alike, and the device's own report shows they are not. 152 is also what GB300 reports (hardware/gb300.yaml), at the same count for a different compute capability. This is a PER-GPU figure, not a per-rack one: the 72 GPUs of the NVL72 domain give the rack 10,944 SMs, but the cost model reads this field per device. The cost model reads SMCount for the derate a concurrent KV fetch causes: the 12 SMs a Triton-path fetch withholds while it overlaps a forward pass (cost model §8.3), which is 7.89% at 152 SMs and was 8.11% at the 148 this entry carried.

_comment_cc ComputeCapability is the CUDA compute capability NVIDIA lists for this part (https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus). A model graph that differs by GPU generation resolves its architecture overlay by the major version, so a chip that states none cannot run such a graph.

gb300: provenance notes

_comment GB300 (Grace-Blackwell Ultra) in its rack-scale configuration. Peak FLOPs and HBM bandwidth are NVIDIA's per-GPU figures for GB300 NVL72 in the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra Datasheet (document 4169750, Oct 2025; https://resources.nvidia.com/en-us-blackwell-architecture/blackwell-ultra-datasheet, PDF https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/1k0p832eq8r5ca0u5383ie5o4tp3bst1.pdf), table 'Individual Blackwell Ultra GPU Specifications': FP4 '20 PFLOPS | 15 PFLOPS' (sparse | dense), FP8/FP6 10 PFLOPS and FP16/BF16 5 PFLOPS (sparse; 'Dense is ½ sparse spec shown'), giving dense FP4 15000, FP8 5000 and BF16 2500 TFLOPS; and '279 GB HBM3E | 8 TB/s'. AISimulate's descriptor (https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate/blob/2f0f4cd8606d580567b253d02f3d699fe36db865/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/gb300.yaml), which cites that datasheet, carries the same figures. Two things place this part between B300 and GB200. It carries the Blackwell Ultra die (dense FP4 15000 TFLOPS, a 1.5x step over GB200's 10000 and above B300's 14000) at the higher 2500 TFLOPS BF16 rate of the Grace-Blackwell bin rather than B300 SXM's 2250. And it keeps GB200's rack-scale NVLink domain. As on B300, INT8 drops sharply: the datasheet states 330 TOPS sparse (165 dense), and the descriptor's int8_tc_flops of 165 TFLOPS matches it. The catalog has no INT8 field, so none is recorded. MemoryGiB is NOT a datasheet figure: 277.5 GiB is the capacity nvidia-smi reports, as the AISimulate descriptor records it (mem_capacity 298013687808 bytes, '284208MiB reported by nvidia-smi', exactly 284208 MiB). The datasheet states 279 GB. The descriptor's GiB reading is kept rather than converted to decimal GB, the same choice b200 and b300 make, and the opposite of gb200-nvl72, which reads its source's advertised decimal GB.

_comment_memory MemoryGiB is the device total the CUDA driver reports, which is what vLLM v0.31.0 multiplies by gpu_memory_utilization (requested = ceil(total_memory x gmu), vllm/v1/worker/utils.py:539-558), not nvidia-smi's 284208 MiB (277.5 GiB) or the datasheet's 279 GB: 297,020,948,480 B = 276.6223 GiB on 'NVIDIA GB300' (PyTorch CUDACachingAllocator 'total: 297020948480' and vLLM start-up logs 'Free memory on device (273.04/276.62 GiB)', InferenceX DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash GB300 run, https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/38482065647). Measured, not vendor_spec; the rest of this file is vendor_spec, and the MemoryGiB sentence in _comment is superseded by this figure.

_comment_interconnect Like gb200-nvl72 and unlike B200/B300, this part needs three topology tiers rather than two, and for the same reason. IntraNodeBwGBps is the NVLink 5 per-GPU unidirectional figure, 900 GB/s: the datasheet's 'Fifth-Generation NVLink: 1.8 TB/s', bidirectional, halved. A node here is one Grace-Blackwell tray, two Grace CPUs with two GPUs each, so GPUsPerNode is 4, not 8. IntraRackBwGBps is ALSO 900: the descriptor's inter_node_bw (NVLink via NVSwitch within the rack) equals its intra_node_bw, so the NVSwitch fabric spans all 72 GPUs in the rack at full per-GPU bandwidth, and crossing a tray boundary inside the rack is not a bandwidth change at all. Only the rack boundary is, and it is a step down to InfiniBand: the descriptor's inter_rack_bw is 100 GB/s per GPU (CX8 XDR 800 Gb/s; the datasheet states 800 Gb/s of ConnectX-8 networking per GPU), double the gb200-nvl72 rack-boundary reference. That inter-rack fabric is a property of the cluster, not the die, so it lives with the reusable fabric classes rather than here. A GB300 inter-rack scenario names networks/ib-800g.yaml (100 GB/s per GPU), the same fabric B300 names for its inter-node traffic. A model keyed on tp > GPUsPerNode alone would wrongly derate this part: the condition is the link, not the chassis count, and the step is at the rack boundary. The descriptor also states inter_rack_latency: 5 µs, annotated '5us typical for InfiniBand between racks'. That is a typical value rather than a vendor specification, and the catalog has no field for it, so this entry does not record it. No BLIS repository records it today: blis-registry's coefficients/ has no inter-rack latency coefficient, and inference-sim has no flag for one.

_comment_sm SMCount is the count of ENABLED Streaming Multiprocessors per GPU, 152, as the device reports it on GB300 systems. This is NOT a datasheet figure and NOT an NVIDIA publication. The source is FlashInfer's SM103 dispatch-plan tests, which record "Measured SM counts of the dispatch tables ... B200 148, GB300 152 (JHB nodes)" and key the sm_103a plan on 152 (https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/26fe42d91acc1d56bd27560f64e9bf727d623cca/tests/experimental/test_cake_kimi_k3_fp8_projection.py#L65-L66). sm_103a is this part's architecture, matching the AISimulate descriptor's sm_version: 103. The count is what the driver reports for the SKU (cudaDeviceProp.multiProcessorCount); it is not fitted and no workload changes it. No NVIDIA source states it: the AISimulate descriptor states no SM count, NVIDIA's Blackwell Ultra architecture blog states 160 SMs for the FULL two-die implementation and footnotes that available SM count varies by SKU (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/inside-nvidia-blackwell-ultra-the-chip-powering-the-ai-factory-era), and no NVIDIA datasheet gives an enabled count. 152 lies between B300 SXM's 148 (also compute capability 10.3; see hardware/b300.yaml) and the full-die 160. The cost model uses SMCount for two things: the per-SM share of peak FLOPs, and the 12-SM derate a Triton-path KV fetch withholds while it overlaps a forward pass (cost model §8.3), which is 7.89% at 152 SMs.

docs.title: Fabrics
docs.text:
4 inter-node fabric classes, in networks/. A fabric belongs to a cluster, not to a chip, so each is defined once and paired with a chip by the scenario that uses it.

Fabric Description GB/s per GPU RDMA field ib-800g InfiniBand XDR (800 Gb/s) 100 not set ib-400g InfiniBand NDR (400 Gb/s) 50 not set roce-200g RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet, 200 Gb/s) 25 not set ethernet-100gbe Plain Ethernet (100 GbE, TCP, no RDMA) 12.5 not set

Bandwidth is nominal, per GPU and per direction: the line rate of the network cards serving one GPU, converted to gigabytes per second. The fraction a real transfer achieves is a coefficient in the registry. RDMA field shows whether the file sets the optional RDMA key; a file that does not set it makes no claim either way. The catalog states no separate bandwidth for moving a KV cache from a prefill server to a decode server. The kernel's own transfer pricing uses the fabric's figure between nodes; inference-sim currently takes the figure from its --pd-transfer-bandwidth flag.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Each file records the source of its figure, and the conversion applied to it, in its _comment keys. They are reproduced here as written.

ethernet-100gbe: provenance notes

_comment_interconnect Plain Ethernet, TCP/IP (no RDMA): one 100 GbE port per GPU. InterNodeBwGBps is the NOMINAL datasheet figure — 100 Gb/s / 8 = 12.5 GB/s per GPU, per direction — NOT a measurement; TCP typically reaches a smaller fraction of line rate than RDMA (CPU stays in the data path), so real payload throughput runs well below nominal. The measured overhead/correction factor (effective / nominal) is a per-deployment number. It belongs in blis-registry, not in the catalog. blis-registry records no such factor today. The only one it held was pd_transfer_overhead, an assumed 1.0 placeholder, and it was removed with the pd-transfer-estimates set (blis-registry commit 3c9879d). Paired with a chip's on-node IntraNodeBwGBps, only the RATIO prices cross-node collective traffic (#1530); that ratio is a per-deployment (chip + fabric) quantity, resolved wherever a chip and fabric are paired.

_comment_pd_transfer PD KV-transfer over this fabric uses this same InterNodeBwGBps (12.5 GB/s nominal) as its bandwidth — no separate PD figure. The fabric carries no PD base-latency field: the catalog states no inherent fabric base latency, so there is nothing to record here (the nominal figure would only ever be 0). The 0.05 ms PD base latency is a modeling placeholder, not a fabric fact. Today it is inference-sim's --pd-transfer-base-latency default (cmd/root.go) and is recorded in no catalog or registry file. blis-registry PR #16 (for blis-registry#10) moved it into the registry as coefficients/pd-transfer-estimates.yaml on 2026-09-28. That set was later removed (blis-registry commit 3c9879d, 2026-10-05) because no consumer read it. The CLI flags remain the defaults/overrides, so a run that resolves no fabric is byte-identical.

ib-400g: provenance notes

_comment_interconnect InfiniBand NDR: one 400 Gb/s ConnectX-7 NIC per GPU (1:1 GPU:NIC rail), the standard 8-NIC HGX config. InterNodeBwGBps is the NOMINAL datasheet figure — 400 Gb/s / 8 = 50 GB/s per GPU, per direction — NOT a measurement; real RDMA payload throughput runs below nominal. The measured overhead/correction factor (effective / nominal) is a per-deployment number. It belongs in blis-registry, not in the catalog. blis-registry records no such factor today. The only one it held was pd_transfer_overhead, an assumed 1.0 placeholder, and it was removed with the pd-transfer-estimates set (blis-registry commit 3c9879d). Paired with a chip's on-node IntraNodeBwGBps, only the RATIO prices cross-node collective traffic (#1530); that ratio is a per-deployment (chip + fabric) quantity, resolved wherever a chip and fabric are paired.

_comment_pd_transfer PD KV-transfer over this fabric uses this same InterNodeBwGBps as its nominal bandwidth — there is no separate PD bandwidth figure (the old 25 GB/s --pd-transfer-bandwidth default was an implicit roce-200g assumption; see networks/roce-200g.yaml). The fabric carries no PD base-latency field: the catalog states no inherent fabric base latency, so there is nothing to record here (the nominal figure would only ever be 0). The 0.05 ms PD base latency is a modeling placeholder, not a fabric fact. Today it is inference-sim's --pd-transfer-base-latency default (cmd/root.go) and is recorded in no catalog or registry file. blis-registry PR #16 (for blis-registry#10) moved it into the registry as coefficients/pd-transfer-estimates.yaml on 2026-09-28. That set was later removed (blis-registry commit 3c9879d, 2026-10-05) because no consumer read it. The CLI flags remain the defaults/overrides, so a run that resolves no fabric is byte-identical.

ib-800g: provenance notes

_comment_interconnect InfiniBand XDR: one 800 Gb/s ConnectX-8 NIC per GPU (1:1 GPU:NIC rail). InterNodeBwGBps is the NOMINAL line rate — 800 Gb/s / 8 = 100 GB/s per GPU, per direction — NOT a measurement; real RDMA payload throughput runs below nominal. Line-rate evidence: NVIDIA's Blackwell Ultra Datasheet (document 4169750, Oct 2025; PDF https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/1k0p832eq8r5ca0u5383ie5o4tp3bst1.pdf) states 'Blackwell Ultra also features 800 Gbps NVIDIA ConnectX-8 networking, doubling interconnect bandwidth compared to NVIDIA Blackwell', and, for the GB300 NVL72, that the ConnectX-8 SuperNIC IO module 'hosts two ConnectX-8 devices, providing 800 gigabits per second (Gb/s) of network connectivity for each GPU'. The ConnectX-8 SuperNIC user manual (https://networking-docs.nvidia.com/connectx8hw/specifications) lists the single-port OSFP models (C8180, C8180L) at InfiniBand XDR, 'XDR (4 lanes x 200Gb/s per port)', which is 800 Gb/s. Parts that use this class: b300 (HGX B300) and gb300 (its inter-rack fabric); b200, h100 and h200 stay on ib-400g (ConnectX-7). The effective / nominal correction is not stated here; it is registry/coefficients/cost-model-fabric.yaml's fabric_bandwidth_efficiency, which for this class is an assumption (equal to ib-400g's), not a measurement. Paired with a chip's on-node IntraNodeBwGBps, only the RATIO prices cross-node collective traffic (#1530); that ratio is a per-deployment (chip + fabric) quantity, resolved wherever a chip and fabric are paired.

_comment_pd_transfer PD KV-transfer over this fabric uses this same InterNodeBwGBps (100 GB/s nominal) as its nominal bandwidth, as on networks/ib-400g.yaml — there is no separate PD bandwidth figure and no PD base-latency field.

_comment_interconnect RoCE (GPUDirect RDMA over Converged Ethernet): one 200 Gb/s ConnectX RoCE port per GPU. InterNodeBwGBps is the NOMINAL datasheet figure — 200 Gb/s / 8 = 25 GB/s per GPU, per direction — NOT a measurement; real RDMA payload throughput runs below nominal. The measured overhead/correction factor (effective / nominal) is a per-deployment number. It belongs in blis-registry, not in the catalog. blis-registry records no such factor today. The only one it held was pd_transfer_overhead, an assumed 1.0 placeholder, and it was removed with the pd-transfer-estimates set (blis-registry commit 3c9879d). Paired with a chip's on-node IntraNodeBwGBps, only the RATIO prices cross-node collective traffic (#1530); that ratio is a per-deployment (chip + fabric) quantity, resolved wherever a chip and fabric are paired.

_comment_pd_transfer PD KV-transfer over this fabric uses this same InterNodeBwGBps (25 GB/s nominal) as its bandwidth — no separate PD figure. The old 25 GB/s --pd-transfer-bandwidth default was exactly this: a rough guess for a RoCE-200G fabric (≈ half a 400 Gb/s line rate), now made explicit and per-fabric. The fabric carries no PD base-latency field: the catalog states no inherent fabric base latency, so there is nothing to record here (the nominal figure would only ever be 0). The 0.05 ms PD base latency is a modeling placeholder, not a fabric fact. Today it is inference-sim's --pd-transfer-base-latency default (cmd/root.go) and is recorded in no catalog or registry file. blis-registry PR #16 (for blis-registry#10) moved it into the registry as coefficients/pd-transfer-estimates.yaml on 2026-09-28. That set was later removed (blis-registry commit 3c9879d, 2026-10-05) because no consumer read it. The CLI flags remain the defaults/overrides, so a run that resolves no fabric is byte-identical.

docs.title: Router table
docs.text:
3 router modes BLIS does not host, each mapped to the policy of llm-d's router that stands closest to it, in routers/.

BLIS hosts one router, llm-d's, and never simulates another (X4). A benchmark run measured behind another router, such as Dynamo's, is scored by simulating the llm-d policy this table names, and the point says so: it names the router the run used, the policy BLIS used and the evidence below, and it is never graded G1 and never presented as if llm-d had routed the run (point-record kind router_differs). This is design §11.3 and §11.4. A router mode with no entry, or an entry whose policy is none, stays not scored (router_unsupported). An entry whose policy is none records that the mode was examined and no policy is close enough, and says why and what would change that.

An entry whose policy is not none also states each way the mode and the policy differ, each citing the code that shows it, and a measured bound: the largest ratio between the policy and its alternatives for each figure, with the regime it was measured in (workload kind, concurrency range, model, hardware, pool shapes), the evidence file by hash, and what the bound does not cover. The bound is a sensitivity of BLIS's own prediction to the choice of policy. It is not an error against the router's real behaviour, which no run measured. A point scored with the entry copies the differences and the bound, so a reader can decide, figure by figure, whether the substitution is small enough. How the ratios are measured is in the router sensitivity guide.

An entry is added only with evidence: for each field it states, a citation of the router's own code or documentation at a pinned commit, and a citation of llm-d's router code that the policy rests on. A mapping is bound to the builds of the router the entry lists (revisions): a run on another build of the same router and mode has no mapping and stays router_unsupported. The table is keyed by the router, its mode and its session-affinity setting, not by the framework's label, because a router's behaviour is set by its mode. An entry's file is named for its key, <router>-<mode>, with -affinity-<seconds> when the setting is set, so one key cannot be stated twice. Design §11.4 keys it the same way: by the mode and session-affinity setting a run used.

Entry Router Mode Affinity TTL (s) llm-d policy Citations (router / llm-d) Largest ratio dynamo-kv dynamo kv — none 4 / 1 — dynamo-random dynamo random — random-picker 4 / 2 1.70 dynamo-round-robin dynamo round-robin — round-robin 5 / 6 1.65

docs.title: dynamo-kv
docs.text:
Dynamo's kv mode scores each worker by a cost, overlap_score_weight times the blocks of the prompt the worker has not cached plus the decode blocks the router tracks as active on it, with weight 1.0 and temperature 0 by default, so the lowest cost wins and a tie goes to the smaller prefix tree. Both terms are the router's own accounting, fed by the workers' KV events, and the router can hold a request in a queue of its own when the workers are busy (router_queue_threshold). No policy in the closed list does this. least-active-requests reads the router's own in-flight counts but has no prefix term. default adds a prefix term but weighs queue depth and KV-cache utilisation, which llm-d's router reads from its endpoints' metrics, as normalised scores summed with weights 2, 2 and 3, and takes the maximum; Dynamo's cost is in unnormalised block units with the two terms equally weighted per block. The sweep behind the other entries shows the policies that read load differ from each other by up to 1.70 (balanced) and 1.79 (decode-bound) in median time to first token at 64 to 256 clients, default against least-active-requests, so the choice among them is not a rounding. It has no prefix shared between requests, which is the term this mode exists for, so no bound on a stand-in for it can be measured with it. The mode stays unsupported until a composition that carries both terms is hosted and measured on a workload with shared prefixes. A run with session affinity configured is a different key and has no entry.

The router

  • ai-dynamo/dynamo@1682167d3c97:components/src/dynamo/common/configuration/groups/router_args.py:77-84, for the mode: The frontend's router-mode argument accepts kv among its choices, so a recipe can run it.
  • ai-dynamo/dynamo@1682167d3c97:lib/kv-router/src/scheduling/selector.rs:136-143, for the policy: The cost of a worker is overlap_score_weight times its uncached prefill blocks plus its decode blocks, in block units, unnormalised.
  • ai-dynamo/dynamo@1682167d3c97:lib/kv-router/src/scheduling/selector.rs:271-311, for the policy: At temperature 0 the lowest cost wins and a tie goes to the worker with the smaller prefix tree; at a positive temperature a worker is sampled by softmax.
  • ai-dynamo/dynamo@1682167d3c97:lib/kv-router/src/scheduling/config.rs:284-312, for the policy: The defaults are overlap weight 1.0, temperature 0, router-tracked active blocks, router-tracked prefill tokens and a router queue threshold of 4.0.

llm-d's router

  • inference-sim/llm-d-router@b1ab0ff7c0b8:pkg/epp/config/loader/defaults.go:49-90, for the policy: The default configuration sums three scorers, queue depth (weight 2), KV-cache utilisation (2) and prefix cache (3), in one profile with the max-score picker; no scorer there reads the router's own cost of blocks.

docs.title: dynamo-random
docs.text:
Dynamo's random mode and llm-d's random picker do the same thing: for each request, draw a uniform random index over the available workers, with no state between requests and no reading of load. Neither keeps a counter. llm-d's round-robin policy also picks at random among tied endpoints, so the two llm-d policies choose alike; Dynamo's random mode has no dependence on the order of the worker list. The remaining differences are the source of the randomness and the pools each draw serves, below. How far the choice of policy moves BLIS's figures is the bound; the first group of ratios is against round-robin, the other policy that ignores load, and the second against the policies that read load.

Differences

  • draw: Dynamo draws a random 64-bit value from the thread's generator for each request and takes it modulo the number of available instances (push_router.rs 379-392). llm-d's picker shuffles the candidates with the hosted runtime's random source and takes the first (random/picker.go 94-97, common.go 98-104). Both are uniform over the workers and independent between requests. BLIS's source is seeded from the run's seed, so a run is reproducible and is one draw of the sequence; Dynamo's is not seeded, and two runs of it differ in the sequence even on one arrival pattern. (citations 2, 4, 5)
  • pools: Each pool draws on its own in both: Dynamo's prefill and decode routers are separate objects (random keeps no counter to share), and llm-d's random picker draws once for each pick of each profile. No shared state couples the prefill and decode picks. (citations 2, 4)
  • frontends: Several frontends do not change the mode: independent uniform draws merged are still uniform, so Dynamo's mode is the same however many frontends a deployment runs. Nothing here differs on that account. (citations 2)
  • load-blind: Neither reads load, so neither reacts to a worker that falls behind. A policy that does (least-active-requests, default, queue-scorer) is not this mode; the second group of ratios in the bound is what a wrong guess of the mode would cost. (citations 2, 4)

docs.title: dynamo-round-robin
docs.text:
Dynamo's round-robin mode rotates strictly per request: it takes the next value of a counter and indexes the list of available workers by it, so successive requests go to successive workers and every worker gets the same number to within one. llm-d's round-robin policy does not rotate: it is the max-score picker with no scorer, every endpoint is tied, and the picker chooses among the tied endpoints at random (the hosted scheduler shuffles the candidates before each pick), as the random picker does. Neither reads load, so neither reacts to a worker that falls behind, and over a run both spread requests over every endpoint. They differ in the order: Dynamo's is a cycle and llm-d's is a random draw. The nearest llm-d policy picks at random among tied endpoints, and the random picker is equally close, so the first group of the bound is against it. How far the choice of policy moves BLIS's figures is the bound: small for time per output token and for throughput in most of the regime, large for time to first token at 64 to 256 clients when the alternative reads load. An earlier version of this entry held that no policy was close enough because llm-d's counter, drawn at every pick of every profile, would give a prefill pool of even size every other endpoint. The router's own tests and BLIS runs do not show it (the pool-balance difference), and the argument is not made here.

Differences

  • strict-rotation: Dynamo rotates strictly per request (push_router.rs 357-372): the n-th request goes to the instance at n modulo the number of available instances. The nearest llm-d policy picks at random among tied endpoints: the max-score picker rotates the tied candidates by a counter, but they reach it in a seeded random order in a hosted runtime, so the choice is uniformly random, and tests of pools of two, three and four reach every endpoint in near equal counts and not in a cycle. The router has no policy that rotates strictly. The random picker is equally close, and the first group of the bound is against it. These statements are about inference-sim/llm-d-router at commit 03246be994224ef031dfdafb966c54f60d01e933 and no other release; the policy list states none of them. (citations 1, 8, 9, 10)
  • frontends: A Dynamo deployment can run several frontend processes, each with router objects and counters of its own that start at zero, so the sequence of requests a worker sees interleaves independent rotations; the recipes the dashboard read run several (enable_multiple_frontends). BLIS hosts one router and picks at random among tied endpoints. Which frontend a request reaches is the load balancer's choice and is not modelled. (citations 2)
  • pool-balance: Under llm-d's policy a prefill pool is used in full, as the random choice among tied endpoints gives. With a workload that saturates the prefill pool (8,192 prompt tokens, 16 output tokens), round-robin served 25.3 to 27.0 requests per second at 16 to 1,024 clients with two prefill endpoints, against 27.1 to 27.3 under least-active-requests and 13.6 with one prefill endpoint; with four it served 46.3 to 53.3 against 53.6 to 54.4. A pool used through one endpoint would give about half. The 14 percent gap at four endpoints and 16 clients is also seen under the random picker and the default policy, so it is the arrival imbalance of a policy that ignores load. BLIS does not record which prefill endpoint served a request, so the mechanism is not confirmed. The tables are in the guide. (citations 5, 6, 7, 8)
  • load-blind: Neither mode reads load, so neither reacts to a worker that falls behind. A policy that does (least-active-requests, default, queue-scorer) is not this mode; the second group of ratios in the bound is what a wrong guess of the mode would cost. (citations 1, 7)

  • ai-dynamo/dynamo@1682167d3c97:components/src/dynamo/common/configuration/groups/router_args.py:66-68, for the mode: The router-mode argument defaults to round-robin, so a run that sets no router mode runs it.

  • inference-sim/llm-d-router@b1ab0ff7c0b8:pkg/epp/framework/plugins/scheduling/picker/common.go:98-104, for the policy: RandFor returns one source per hosted runtime, shared by every picker of every profile.

docs.title: The policies llm-d's router offers
docs.text:
A policy is a composition of the router's scheduling plugins that it runs without code of BLIS's own. The list is closed and holds names only:

Policy Meaning round-robin every endpoint is treated alike random-picker an endpoint is picked uniformly at random least-active-requests the endpoint with the fewest in-flight requests is preferred default the router's built-in configuration when none is given none no policy is close enough

What a policy is made of (plugins, weights, tie handling, source files) changes with the router's release, so this repository does not list it. The router fork owns it; each entry above states the behaviour it relies on and cites the router tree at the build it names.

The file format, and the rules a validator refuses an entry by, are in the router table reference.

docs.title: Storage tiers
docs.text:
6 tiers a KV cache can be offloaded to, all in devices/storage.yaml.

Tier What it is Registry coefficients cpu_dram Pinned host DRAM, reached across the host link offload_tier_cpu_dram_read_rate, _write_rate, _base_latency nvme_gen3 A PCIe Gen3 NVMe drive, as a class and not a product offload_tier_nvme_gen3_read_rate, _write_rate, _base_latency nvme_gen4 A PCIe Gen4 NVMe drive, as a class and not a product offload_tier_nvme_gen4_read_rate, _write_rate, _base_latency nvme_gen4_raid0_8x A DGX/HGX H100 node's local NVMe data volume offload_tier_nvme_gen4_raid0_8x_read_rate, _write_rate, _base_latency s3 An object store reached over the network, as a class and not a product offload_tier_s3_read_rate, _write_rate, _base_latency sata_ssd A SATA SSD, as a class and not a product offload_tier_sata_ssd_read_rate, _write_rate, _base_latency

A tier is a name and a description. The catalog states no rate and no latency for it, because each such figure was fitted to one host's measurements or chosen as a representative value, and neither is a declared fact of a device. The kernel prices a transfer as the larger of the tier's base latency and the bytes divided by its rate, so the base latency decides the cost of small transfers, and it reads the three terms from the coefficient registry, where each is scoped to the hardware it describes and carries its method and evidence. See the cost-model-offload-tiers reference for every value and how the tier coefficients are written.

docs.title: Workloads
docs.text: 7 workloads, in two forms. A shape says how long requests are, not how many arrive; the arrival rate or concurrency is set by each run. A replay workload names a load generator's trace-replay scenario over a pinned corpus; the corpus decides the requests, and each run sets the number of lanes.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Each replay file records its provenance in its _comment keys. They are reproduced here as written.

agentx-mvp: provenance notes

_comment Provenance: the agentic workload our calibration runs benchmark with, aiperf 0.12.0 --scenario inferencex-agentx-mvp over the public-dataset alias semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126_256k (inference-sim/blis-catalog#34). The corpus is not vendored: a consumer fetches traces.jsonl from the Hugging Face dataset semianalysisai/cc-traces-weka-062126-256k at the pinned revision and checks it against sha256 before replaying it. A real aiperf 0.12.0 run does not pin the revision: the alias's plugin metadata sets hf_dataset_name and hf_split but no hf_revision (plugin/plugins.yaml:2429-2447), so the loader reads the dataset's HEAD (dataset/loader/base_hf_dataset.py:77), and aiperf exposes no CLI flag to override it (--tokenizer-revision is the tokenizer's). A run that claims this workload must therefore check the downloaded traces.jsonl against sha256. The lane count (aiperf --concurrency) is each run's choice, so it is stated where the workload is bound, not here.

_comment_corpus Corpus: Apache-2.0, ungated. traces.jsonl is 568,864,747 bytes. The dataset's stats.txt at the pinned revision states 393 traces, 28,444 main turns, 1,697 subagent groups, 39,822 subagent inner requests, 68,266 model requests, 6,891,228,864 input tokens and 58,728,807 output tokens. Its README.md says it was built on 2026-06-21 by utils/agentic/build_weka_hf_dataset.py from semianalysisai/cc-traces-weka-062126 (SemiAnalysis Claude Code proxy traces, trace version 7 only), capping each request at 256,000 input + output tokens.

_comment_run Run settings, as our calibration runs use them: random_seed 42 (aiperf alone would draw a random seed); benchmark_duration_s 900, the scenario's floor (its default is 1800); grace_period_s 30, aiperf's --benchmark-grace-period default, which the scenario does not set; max_context_length max_model_len, the deployment's resolved --max-model-len, which drops every trace whose recorded peak prompt plus output exceeds it.

_comment_locked cache_bust, system_idle_gap_cap_s, trajectory_start, warmup and split_flattened_agents are stated at the values aiperf 0.12.0 applies under the scenario (common/scenario/inferencex_agentx_mvp.py; common/environment.py WEKA_SPLIT_FLATTENED_AGENTS), so the file reads as the whole run. category coding is the corpus plugin's default_prompt_corpus, and thinking on is the THINKING_MODE InferenceX's benchmark workflows set (InferenceX 9fa76586 .github/workflows/benchmark-tmpl.yml:96), which its launcher requires for speculative AgentX throughput runs (inferencex-e2e/infx/launch/request.py:141-146); together they select the acceptance profile.

agentx-mvp-uncapped: provenance notes

_comment Provenance: the agentic workload InferenceX replays for most models, aiperf 0.12.0 --scenario inferencex-agentx-mvp over the public-dataset alias semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126, the uncapped corpus (inference-sim/blis-catalog#49). It is agentx-mvp with only the corpus changed: agentx-mvp replays the 256k-capped corpus, and this entry keeps the requests over 256k tokens that fill a 1M-token KV pool. The corpus is not vendored: a consumer fetches traces.jsonl from the Hugging Face dataset semianalysisai/cc-traces-weka-062126 at the pinned revision and checks it against sha256 before replaying it. A real aiperf 0.12.0 run does not pin the revision: the alias's plugin metadata sets hf_dataset_name and hf_split but no hf_revision (plugin/plugins.yaml:2409-2427), so the loader reads the dataset's HEAD (dataset/loader/base_hf_dataset.py:77), and aiperf exposes no CLI flag to override it (--tokenizer-revision is the tokenizer's). A run that claims this workload must therefore check the downloaded traces.jsonl against sha256. The lane count (aiperf --concurrency) is each run's choice, so it is stated where the workload is bound, not here.

_comment_corpus Corpus: Apache-2.0 (the dataset card's license field), ungated. traces.jsonl is 1,847,151,435 bytes, 3.2 times the capped corpus. The dataset's stats.txt at the pinned revision states 393 traces, 56,798 main turns, 1,697 subagent groups, 42,029 subagent inner requests, 98,827 model requests, 21,635,381,376 input tokens and 106,474,498 output tokens. Its README.md says it was built on 2026-06-21 by utils/agentic/build_weka_hf_dataset.py from SemiAnalysis Claude Code proxy traces (trace version 7 only), and that each request's input is capped at 990,016 tokens to drop KV-cache-block overcount artifacts; there is no 256k cap.

Earlier commits had the opposite default, so this rule holds only at that commit. The corpus a run actually loaded, read from its recorded aiperf command (--public-dataset), decides which entry it is scored with: semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126 is this entry, semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126_256k is agentx-mvp.

docs.title: Using the catalog
docs.text:
A run of BLIS uses the catalog embedded in the blis-substrate release it was built with, or a directory you name instead. It never downloads catalog data and never writes to it.

To use the catalog:

  1. Use the embedded copy, or name a directory. Point BLIS at the catalog gives the flags, how a run names the entries it needs, and what each result records about the catalog it used.
  2. Read the formats of your release. The loaders parse catalog files strictly, so a directory named with --catalog must match the formats of the simulator's substrate release. Releases and pinning explains why.
  3. Experiment in a copy. To try a hypothetical model or chip, edit a copy of the catalog and name it when you run. Experiment with a candidate catalog shows how.

docs.title: Experiment with a candidate catalog
docs.text: To ask what BLIS predicts for a model or a chip that is not in a release, edit a copy of the catalog and name the copy when you run. You need no fork of the simulator, no rebuild and no pull request.

docs.title: Edit a copy
docs.text:
Start from a working tree of blis-substrate, or a copy of its catalog/ directory, and edit it. If you edit a model's config.json, derive its graph again, so that graph.yaml matches the edited config; the cost model reads graph.yaml, not config.json. Then validate the directory, so that a malformed edit fails here rather than in the middle of a run. From the repository root:

pip install --require-hashes -r catalog/scripts/requirements-dev.txt
python3 catalog/scripts/derive_graph.py --model qwen3-14b
go run ./validate/cmd/validate-catalog catalog

Both take any directory with the catalog's layout, so a copy elsewhere is derived and checked the same way:

python3 catalog/scripts/derive_graph.py ~/scratch/catalog-wide-heads --model qwen3-14b
go run ./validate/cmd/validate-catalog ~/scratch/catalog-wide-heads

docs.title: Run with it
docs.text:
Name the edited directory with --catalog; the run uses it instead of the embedded catalog:

blis run --scenario path/to/scenario.yaml --catalog ~/scratch/catalog-wide-heads

To run a private model against the released data, put only its entry in a directory, for example models/<name>/, and add it with --catalog-overlay <dir>. The rest of the catalog stays the embedded copy. Point BLIS at the catalog states how overlay entries replace or add to the data.

docs.title: An experiment is labelled
docs.text: The Result records the catalog's source as path, with its content hash and the hash of any overlay. Its data are not the release's embedded data, so the run is experimental, and its figures cannot be mistaken for, or published as, those of a release (What a result records). To let others reproduce the experiment, commit the edits and publish the commit, for example on a fork; the content hash then names data anyone can fetch and check.

docs.title: Point BLIS at the catalog
docs.text: A run of BLIS uses the catalog embedded in the blis-substrate release the simulator was built with. There is nothing to clone or install: a released blis binary carries the exact catalog it was tested with.

docs.title: Where a run's catalog comes from
docs.text:
Each run reads one catalog, from one of two sources (design §3.3):

The embedded copy When no catalog is named, the run uses the data compiled into the substrate release. A path --catalog <dir>, or the BLIS_CATALOG environment variable, names a directory with the same layout as catalog/ in blis-substrate: a working tree, a copy of it, or an exported revision. The run uses that directory instead of the embedded copy.

To add entries to the catalog in use rather than replace it, --catalog-overlay <dir> names a directory of additions. An overlay entry is a whole model directory (models/<name>/), or a whole hardware, device, network or workload file. An entry with the same identity as an existing one replaces it; any other entry is added. The combined catalog is then validated in full. An overlay may not contain ledger files.

The catalog flags and the registry flags (--registry, --registry-overlay) are independent. A run may, for example, use the embedded catalog with a candidate registry.

Whatever its source, the catalog is validated when it is loaded, by the same validators CI runs, including the checks between catalog and registry. A model runs only if it is in the catalog in use. A missing model is refused with the catalog's source (the embedded release, or a path) and the relative path its entry belongs at. No run creates or changes catalog files, and no run fetches anything from the network.

docs.title: How a run names its entries
docs.text:
A run is described by a scenario file. It holds two YAML documents. The Scenario names the model, the chip, the fabric and the coefficient sets. The Deployment states, for each pool, its role, its node count, its parallelism and its engine settings. A pool is one serving engine. A colocated pool runs prefill and decode together; a disaggregated deployment has separate prefill and decode pools. You supply the scenario; the catalog supplies the facts its names refer to, and the registry supplies the coefficients.

blis run --scenario path/to/deepseek-v3-h200-fp8-sglang-tp8.yaml

An abridged scenario file:

kind: Scenario
name: deepseek-v3-h200-fp8-sglang-tp8
engine_version: "0.29.0"           # the engine rules pack to validate against
model: deepseek-v3                 # models/deepseek-v3/graph.yaml
coefficients: [cost-model-primitives, cost-model-collectives, ...]
cluster:
  hardware: h200                   # hardware/h200.yaml
  nodes: 1
  gpus_per_node: 8
  # fabric: ib-400g                # networks/ib-400g.yaml; for a multi-node cluster
---
kind: Deployment
name: deepseek-v3-h200-fp8-sglang-tp8
pools:
  - role: colocated
    nodes: 1
    parallel: {tp: 8, pp: 1, dp: 1, enable_expert_parallel: false}
    engine: {quantization: fp8, ...}

Every name is a path under the catalog root, used exactly as written:

The scenario names The cost model reads model: deepseek-v3 models/deepseek-v3/graph.yaml cluster.hardware: h200 hardware/h200.yaml cluster.fabric: ib-400g, when present networks/ib-400g.yaml (always) devices/storage.yaml

The cost model prices the model's model graph. No runtime code reads a model's config.json; every model value a run needs is a field of the graph (SUB-3). Each file is loaded strictly, so a misspelled key is an error rather than a silent zero.

inference-sim reads catalog data only through blis-substrate's loader, so every file a run reads, including a workload shape named with --workload and the storage tiers that KV-cache offload names, comes from the catalog in use and is validated the same way.

docs.title: What a result records
docs.text:
Every run computes a content hash of the catalog it used: the SHA-256 of a sorted list of every data file's SHA-256 and its path. The Result document records, for the catalog and for the registry:

  • its source: embedded or path;
  • its content hash;
  • the hash of each overlay, and the hash of the combined data.

It also records the build the simulator came from: a tagged release, or unreleased. A run uses released data only when the simulator is a tagged release, the catalog and registry hashes equal that release's embedded hashes, and no overlay is used. Every other run is experimental. Only released-data results are published (X8).

docs.title: Releases and pinning
docs.text: The catalog is released with the rest of blis-substrate: a git tag vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH on main (design §14.1), with a GitHub release whose notes say what changed. A release embeds its catalog, so a simulator built on that release reads exactly those files unless a run names another catalog directory.

docs.title: What a version promises
docs.text:
A PATCH release changes no contract, price or value. A new model, chip or field, or a changed figure, is a MINOR release whose notes list what changed. Every Result records the catalog's source and content hash, so a figure can be traced to the data behind it.

To see what moved between two releases:

git diff v0.11.0 v0.12.0 --stat -- catalog/

docs.title: Why a path must match the release
docs.text: The loaders parse the catalog strictly. An unknown key is an error, not a field to ignore, because an ignored field reads as zero, and a zero peak rate or token count gives a plausible but wrong result with no warning. A simulator therefore reads the catalog formats of the substrate release it was built with. A directory named with --catalog must be in those formats: a catalog from a newer release that adds or renames a key is refused at load, with the file and the key.

docs.title: Which docs version to read
docs.text:
The version menu at the top of this site has one entry per MAJOR.MINOR line, and each entry describes the newest patch release on that line. latest is the highest release. dev describes main and changes with every merge. Pre-releases are not published.

This page describes the main branch, which is not a release.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text: BLIS, the Blackbox Inference Simulator, estimates how an LLM serving deployment will perform before anyone runs it. The contracts, the packages under contracts/ in blis-substrate, define the documents BLIS reasons about and check them: types for a model, its hardware, the coefficients a cost model uses, a deployment, its traffic and a measured run; a validator for each; the interface a cost model implements; the interface an engine implements; and the contract between a simulator and the request router it hosts. They hold no data. Every Go repository in BLIS imports them.

docs.title: The idea in brief
docs.text:
A document's shape is defined here. Its contents live in the catalog, in the registry, or in the scenario and deployment a user writes. A scenario fixes the problem: the model, the hardware, the traffic, and the engine version. A deployment states the choices made against it: parallelism, engine settings, offload. Validation asks two questions and keeps the answers apart. Is each document well formed? That never depends on an engine release. Would the release the scenario names run it as written? That always does. Every validator reports every problem at once, each naming the field that is wrong.

The BLIS repositories and the contracts blis-substrate is one Go module with five directories. kernel/ and validate/ import the contracts/ packages; kernel/ reads catalog/ and registry/, and validate/ checks them. blis-vllm, blis-sglang and the llm-d router fork import only the contracts/ packages. inference-sim imports the whole substrate module, each engine and the router fork. blis-substrate · one Go module contracts/ types, validators, interfaces catalog/ declared facts · YAML registry/ coefficients · YAML kernel/ the cost model validate/ data validators blis-vllm implements Engine blis-sglang implements Engine llm-d router fork implements the router contract contracts/ only inference-sim the simulator the whole module engines, router Solid: Go import, pointing at what is imported. Dotted: files the cost model reads. Dashed: files the validators check. Who imports what. The engine repositories and the router fork import only the packages under contracts/, so a coefficient or pricing change needs no engine or router release. inference-sim imports the whole substrate module, each engine and the router fork. The packages under contracts/ import only the Go standard library, the YAML parser and each other.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• You edit catalog or registry data

    Run the validators CI runs on catalog/ and registry/, and look up what a key means.

    Validate the catalog and the registry · Reference

  • You write Go that reads these documents

    Load documents, validate them together, and read the report.

    Validate documents from Go · Kernel interface · Router contract

  • You want to know why it is built this way

    The ideas the contracts rest on, then the reasoning behind particular choices.

    Concepts · Design notes

  • You are changing the contracts

    Where a change belongs, how it is tested, and the rule that contracts change only compatibly.

    Contributing

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go get github.com/inference-sim/blis-substrate@<version>

The packages are imported by path, such as github.com/inference-sim/blis-substrate/contracts/spec/scenario. From the root of a blis-substrate checkout, the validators check the repository's own data:

go run ./validate/cmd/validate-catalog catalog
go run ./validate/cmd/validate-registry registry

These pages are versioned. The selector in the header switches between release lines; dev follows the main branch.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Four short pages: where things live, what the documents are, how they are checked, and the rules every document follows. Read them in order if you are new. The terms below are used with one meaning throughout.

The BLIS repositories What each of the seven repositories owns, and what each takes from the contracts. Documents The eleven kinds of document, where each lives, and how they refer to each other. Validation The two questions a validator asks, why they are kept apart, and what a report holds. Contracts Where a document's name comes from, how units are written, why an unknown key is an error.

docs.title: The project
docs.text: BLIS The Blackbox Inference Simulator: a simulator for LLM serving, made of the seven repositories described in The BLIS repositories. catalog The catalog, catalog/ in blis-substrate: models, chips, fabrics, storage classes and workload shapes, each a fact someone wrote down. registry The registry, registry/ in blis-substrate: coefficient sets, the numbers a cost model uses, each with how it was obtained and where it holds. cost model A function from a batch of requests and a deployment to memory use and the time of one forward pass. To price something is to compute that time or memory for it. kernel A cost model seen through the Kernel interface defined here. The cost model in kernel/ implements it. The word also appears in its ordinary GPU sense, as in "an all-reduce kernel"; the context always says which.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text: scenario The problem a run is given: a model, the cluster it may use, the traffic it serves, the coefficient sets that price it, and the engine version. Designs compared for one problem share one scenario. deployment The choices made against a scenario: how the cluster is divided into pools, each pool's parallel layout and engine settings, the offload tiers, and how KV moves from prefill to decode. A search over designs varies the deployment and leaves the scenario alone. pool The nodes that serve one role (colocated, prefill or decode) with one layout and one set of engine settings. A pool may run several engine instances. storage class, offload tier A storage class is a kind of device, such as cpu_dram or nvme_gen4, described in the catalog. An offload tier is a deployment's use of one storage class for KV, with a capacity.

docs.title: Serving
docs.text: engine, engine version The serving engine is the software that runs the model; vLLM today. A scenario's engine version is the exact release string, such as 0.29.0, of the engine whose behavior the run describes. Its coefficients are fitted against that release, and it selects the rules pack. prefill, decode Prefill is the forward pass over a request's prompt. Decode is each later step, which produces one token (or, with speculative decoding, a few). A deployment may run them on the same pool (colocated) or on separate pools (disaggregated). KV cache The attention keys and values an engine keeps for each request's tokens between steps. It is most of a request's memory, and moving it is most of the cost of disaggregation. rank One GPU's share of an engine. An engine has one rank per GPU. parallel widths How an engine divides work across ranks. tp, tensor parallelism, splits each layer's matrices. pp, pipeline parallelism, splits the layers into stages. dp, data parallelism, runs replicas. pcp and dcp, prefill- and decode-context parallelism, split one request's context. ep, expert parallelism, spreads a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model's experts and is derived from the others. See Parallel layouts.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: field layer, rule layer The two layers of validation. The field layer finds field problems: a document is malformed whatever engine runs it. The rule layer finds rule problems: the named engine release would refuse the document, or would run it differently from what it says. rules pack The checks and accepted values for one engine release. The engine model that owns the release owns its pack, and a caller passes it to a validator. problem One thing a validator reports, at a path such as pools[0].parallel.dcp, with a severity: an error, which fails validation, or a warning, which does not.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text: Each document type has its own keys, but all of them follow a few common rules. Each rule exists to stop a document from looking correct while meaning something its author did not intend.

docs.title: A name has one source
docs.text:
A document's identity comes from one place:

  • A chip, a fabric and a workload shape are named by their file: hardware/h100.yaml is the chip h100. The file has no name key, and one placed there is rejected.
  • A storage class is named by its key in devices/storage.yaml.
  • A model is named by its directory under models/. Its graph.yaml and model.yaml repeat the name in a name key, and validate-catalog fails if either differs from the directory.
  • A coefficient set is referred to by its file name under coefficients/, and its name key matches it by convention.
  • A scenario, a deployment and an evaluation run carry their name in a name key.

Two independent sources for one name would eventually disagree, and a reader could not tell which was meant.

docs.title: A unit is part of the key
docs.text:
Where a number has a unit, the key the author types names it: ttft_ms, IntraNodeBwGBps, BwPeakTBs. A unit stated only in a Go field name or in a comment is invisible to whoever writes the YAML. An author who copies a datasheet figure given in milliseconds into a field that expects microseconds would pass every check and be wrong by a factor of a thousand.

There are three exceptions, each with its own reason:

  • In Go, durations are time.Duration, which carries its unit.
  • A coefficient's value has its unit in a separate units key, because a coefficient set holds quantities of many dimensions. units takes one of a fixed list of values.
  • A trace header has an explicit time_unit key, because the timestamps live in a separate file and the tools that write traces spell the unit differently.

Adding a unit key beside a key that already names its unit, such as ttft_unit: ms next to ttft_ms, is ruled out. It would be a second source that can disagree with the first.

docs.title: An unknown key is an error
docs.text:
Every loader decodes strictly. A key the type does not declare fails the load, and the error names it. Otherwise misspelling max_num_seqs as max_num_seq would produce a document that loads, validates and lacks the setting its author meant to make. Nothing would report the mistake.

Two kinds of key are allowed without being declared:

  • Catalog comments. The catalog annotates its numbers with prose. In chip, fabric and workload-shape files, and inside each storage class, a key that is exactly _comment or begins with _comment_ is accepted and discarded. No other underscore-prefixed key is accepted, so a fitted factor cannot slip into a datasheet file disguised as a comment.
  • A redundant name. Inside a storage class or a coefficient entry, a name key is accepted and then replaced by the class's key or the entry's map key. It cannot change the identity.

docs.title: Vocabularies are closed
docs.text:
An enumerated value must be one the schema lists. An unrecognized unit, evidence method, attention kind or dtype is an error. Whether a coefficient was measured or assumed is recorded in its method, and that record means something only if method takes one of a fixed list of values. The lists are in Vocabularies.

Names that belong to an engine release, such as backend names, cache dtypes and quantization methods, are different. They change from release to release, so the release's rules pack checks them, not the schema. See Validation.

docs.title: Numbers are finite
docs.text:
Every floating-point value must be finite. A NaN compares false to every bound and +Inf looks positive, so either would pass a range check and corrupt every calculation that used it. The loaders reject both before a range is checked, and -Inf with them.

One kind of field is the exception: a number whose meaning includes "no limit". Such a field says so in its Go type with the struct tag infinity:"allowed", and holds +Inf, written .inf in YAML. Today that is grace_period_s alone, where .inf waits indefinitely. NaN and -Inf are refused in it as everywhere. A JSON Result has no infinity, so it writes the string "inf" for such a field and reads it back; the string is that field's infinity and nothing else's.

docs.title: Zero means unset, except in tri-state keys
docs.text:
Most optional numeric keys treat zero as "not stated": a block_size of 0 means the engine chooses. That works because no meaningful value of those keys is zero.

Where false or zero is a meaningful value distinct from silence, the key is tri-state. enable_prefix_caching is the clearest case. vLLM enables prefix caching by default, so a deployment that omits the key describes one with caching, and enable_prefix_caching: false describes one without it. In Go these keys are pointers. In YAML, leaving the key out is the third state.

docs.title: A request is not a resolution
docs.text: Some deployment settings are requests the engine may override. A deployment records what was asked for. A cost model reports what it resolved, and each request it overrode, in its Resolution. The reasoning is in Where the kernel stops.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
The contracts define eleven kinds of YAML document. A run needs two that its user writes, a scenario and a deployment. They refer by name to documents committed in the catalog and the registry.

How the documents refer to each other A scenario names catalog entries by key: model, cluster.hardware, cluster.fabric, cluster.storage and workload.shape, and names registry coefficient sets under coefficients. A deployment is applied to a scenario. An evaluation run names the scenario it measured. catalog/ Model graph models/<name>/ Chip hardware/<name>.yaml Fabric networks/<name>.yaml Storage classes devices/storage.yaml Workload shape workloads/<name>.yaml Scenario the problem, fixed: model, cluster, traffic, coefficients, engine version model cluster.hardware cluster.fabric cluster.storage workload.shape registry/ Coefficient sets coefficients/<name>.yaml coefficients Deployment the choices, varied made against Evaluation run a measurement scenario A scenario refers to everything else by name. Each arrow is labeled with the scenario key that holds the name. A deployment names catalog entries in one place only: each offload tier names a storage class, which must be one the scenario's cluster lists, if the cluster lists any.

docs.title: The problem and the choices
docs.text:
A scenario states what is given: the model, the cluster it runs on, the traffic it serves, the coefficient sets that price it, and the engine version. Nothing in a scenario is a decision. Two candidate designs for the same problem share one scenario.

A deployment states what is decided. It divides the cluster into pools, gives each pool a parallel layout and engine settings, and describes the offload tiers and the transfer of KV cache from prefill to decode. A search over designs varies the deployment and leaves the scenario alone.

The two are separate documents because they change at different rates and for different reasons. Neither carries the load level. Request rate or concurrency is swept by the run and recorded with its results.

A scenario
kind: Scenario
name: llama-3.1-8b-on-h100
model: llama-3.1-8b-instruct
coefficients:
  - cost-model-primitives
  - cost-model-collectives
  - cost-model-host-overheads
  - cost-model-attention
  - cost-model-recurrent
engine:
  kind: vllm
  version: "0.29.0"
workload:
  shape: chatbot
cluster:
  hardware: h100
  nodes: 1
  gpus_per_node: 8
A deployment made against it
kind: Deployment
name: tp2-dp4
pools:
  - role: colocated
    nodes: 1
    parallel:
      tp: 2
      pp: 1
      dp: 4
    engine:
      block_size: 16
      max_num_seqs: 256
      max_num_batched_tokens: 8192
      gpu_memory_utilization: 0.9

docs.title: The eleven kinds
docs.text:
Document Lives in Its name comes from Reference Scenario wherever its user keeps it its name key Scenario Deployment wherever its user keeps it its name key Deployment Model graph catalog, models/<name>/graph.yaml the directory name, repeated in its name key Model graph Model identity catalog, models/<name>/model.yaml the directory name, repeated in its name key Model graph Chip catalog, hardware/<name>.yaml the file name Hardware Fabric catalog, networks/<name>.yaml the file name Hardware Storage classes catalog, devices/storage.yaml each class's key in the file Hardware Workload shape or replay workload catalog, workloads/<name>.yaml the file name Workload Coefficient set registry, coefficients/<name>.yaml the file name, which a scenario uses; its name key matches by convention Coefficient set Acceptance-profile set registry, acceptance/<name>.yaml the file name, which a scenario's acceptance.profiles uses; its name key matches by convention Acceptance profiles Evaluation run wherever its user keeps it its name key Evaluation run Measured run catalog, measurements/<license_ref>/<name>.yaml its name key, which must match the file name Measured run Licence registry catalog, measurements/sources.yaml each source's id Measured run

A model entry in the catalog is a directory. It holds an identity manifest recording where the model's configuration came from and, once the catalog has derived it, a graph of the GPU work a forward pass launches. Beside them sits the vendor's own config.json. It belongs to the vendor, so it has no schema here and is checked only for being a non-empty JSON object.

docs.title: References are names
docs.text:
A scenario never contains a chip or a model. It contains the name of one, and the name is resolved against a catalog checkout when the scenario is used. This keeps a scenario short, and a correction to the catalog reaches every scenario that names the corrected entry.

It also means a scenario can be well formed and still name something that does not exist. hardware: nvidia-h100 is a valid string; the catalog calls that chip h100. Checking that each name resolves is a separate step, described in Validation.

docs.title: Traffic at two fidelities
docs.text: A scenario's workload takes one of two forms. A shape names a catalog workload, which describes traffic as distributions: mean prompt and output lengths, their spread and bounds, and one shared prefix length. A trace points to a captured file of real requests, with their own lengths, arrival times and prefix structure; see Workload. A scenario that asks only a capacity question omits workload.

docs.title: Evaluation runs
docs.text: An evaluation run records what a benchmark measured. For each concurrency level it gives the throughput, the time to first token, the inter-token latency, and optionally KV utilization and cache hit rate. It names the scenario it measured, so a prediction for that scenario can be compared with it.

docs.title: The BLIS repositories
docs.text:
BLIS is seven repositories. blis-substrate holds what is true whatever engine runs: the contracts, the catalog, the registry and the cost model. The contracts, the packages under contracts/, hold no data and run no simulation. They define the documents the repositories exchange, the checks those documents must pass, and the interfaces between the Go repositories.

The BLIS repositories and the contracts blis-substrate is one Go module with five directories. kernel/ and validate/ import the contracts/ packages; kernel/ reads catalog/ and registry/, and validate/ checks them. blis-vllm, blis-sglang and the llm-d router fork import only the contracts/ packages. inference-sim imports the whole substrate module, each engine and the router fork. blis-substrate · one Go module contracts/ types, validators, interfaces catalog/ declared facts · YAML registry/ coefficients · YAML kernel/ the cost model validate/ data validators blis-vllm implements Engine blis-sglang implements Engine llm-d router fork implements the router contract contracts/ only inference-sim the simulator the whole module engines, router Solid: Go import, pointing at what is imported. Dotted: files the cost model reads. Dashed: files the validators check. Who imports what. The engine repositories and the router fork import only the packages under contracts/, so a coefficient or pricing change needs no engine or router release. inference-sim imports the whole substrate module, each engine and the router fork. The packages under contracts/ import only the Go standard library, the YAML parser and each other.
