  • independent re-derivation — re-runs the fitter and compares to the registry, so a value edited without its citation fails.
  • single-sourced citations — every source in the AISimulate sets must cite AISimulate.
  • lane pinning — the all-reduce test pins the vllm_graph lane specifically, because eager is SLOWER than NCCL and accepting either would accept a 3.4x mispricing.
  • memory occupancy — emit_memory.py --check re-renders cost-model-memory.yaml byte for byte when the AISimulate tree is present; its capture half re-derives from the committed CSV in CI with no tree at all, and property tests hold every vLLM cudagraph_mode to an entry, no capturing mode above FULL_AND_PIECEWISE, and the activation multiple non-increasing with width and at least as large for MoE as for dense (§11).
  • skips are explicit — a gate that cannot run says why. The three-factor GEMM ramp's gate skips while the registry carries the one-factor form, and activates the moment the coefficients land.

docs.title: 7. Held-out validation of the lane decisions
docs.text: §4 states the splitting principle. This section records the folds actually run, the numbers they produced, and the decisions they support or refuse. Every figure here is reproduced by the script named beside it; none is a residual on the rows that were fitted.

docs.title: 7.1 Sliding-window attention: hold out one window width
docs.text:
scripts/holdout_attention_swa.py. The window is the dimension that defines the kind — kv_bytes reads min(context, window) positions — so a held-out width is a byte count the fit never saw. Reported as the median over folds, because the widths are heavily unbalanced (window 128 carries 82% of h200's rows, so that fold trains on an eighth of the sweep while the others hold out 3-6%); a mean over folds this uneven would describe none of them.

part vLLM collection vLLM median held-out TRT-LLM median held-out shared folds won by vLLM decision h200 vllm/0.25.0 1.457x 1.754x 3/3 relane h100 vllm/0.25.0 1.433x 1.787x 2/2 relane b200 vllm/0.25.0 1.344x 1.475x 2/3 relane b300 vllm/0.25.0 1.317x 1.498x 2/2 relane gb200-nvl72 vllm/0.25.0 1.276x 1.358x 3/3 relane l40s vllm/0.24.0 2.073x 1.681x 0/2 relane, at a stated cost (5be809b)

Twelve of thirteen shared folds favour vLLM on the five relaned parts; the single exception is b200 at window 2048 (1.259x against 1.244x). The vLLM sweep also covers five widths where TRT-LLM covers two or three, so the TRT-LLM fit was never tested at 512 or 1024 on any part.

L40S is the documented exception and has held-out evidence rather than a residual: its vLLM fit is worse on BOTH folds. It was relaned anyway, deliberately, in 5be809b: the decision rule there was lane correctness — one engine per predicted step — with the fit penalty recorded rather than hidden, and relane_attention_swa.py --check now maintains the L40S and GB300 pairs alongside the five 0.25.0 parts. An earlier revision of this paragraph and of that script's header said L40S stayed on TRT-LLM. Note that L40S has no vllm/0.25.0 attention collection at all — vllm/0.24.0 is its newest — so the comparison uses that, and an earlier reading of "no vLLM data" for this part was wrong.

docs.title: 7.2 KDA: hold out the head-count geometry
docs.text:
scripts/fit_recurrent.py --group-by kernel+heads. vLLM's KDA sweep varies num_k_heads over 12/24/48/96 where SGLang's holds it at 12. Pooling those four geometries into one fit gives geo-err 1.733x; fitted per geometry the same rows give 1.169x to 1.196x. The pooled figure is an artefact of the pooling, not a property of the lane:

lane num_k_heads n floor rate geo-err sglang/0.5.16 (committed) 12 11 5.1 us 1.50 tok/us 1.160x vllm/0.1.dev19262 12 11 5.4 us 1.75 tok/us 1.169x vllm/0.1.dev19262 24 11 5.3 us 1.00 tok/us 1.196x vllm/0.1.dev19262 48 11 3.6 us 0.50 tok/us 1.191x vllm/0.1.dev19262 96 11 3.6 us 0.25 tok/us 1.188x

At the matching geometry — num_k_heads: 12, which is what SGLang measures — the two lanes are equivalent (1.160x against 1.169x, a difference of 0.009). An earlier claim that the vLLM lane fits 1.49x worse was wrong, and wrong because of the pooling above.

This does not by itself relane KDA. The vLLM collection is a dev build (0.1.dev19262+gb6bbf29dd), Kimi-K3 appears in no InferenceX tier and in no FPM artifact with a KDA node, so the change is unevaluable end to end and the decision rests on fit quality alone, where the two lanes tie.

docs.title: 7.3 GEMM ramp: hold out whole K values, and the largest M values
docs.text:
scripts/holdout_gemm_ramp.py. Two folds, and the second one found a defect in the FORM rather than in the lane.

The ramp is the wrong shape above M ~ 4096. eff(M) = eps_max * M / (M + M_half) is monotone and saturating, but the measured envelope PEAKS mid-sweep and then declines — on h200 bfloat16, 0.956 at M=3329 falling to 0.875 at M=32768 on the vLLM lane, and 0.870 at M=4097 falling to 0.839 on TRT-LLM. Both lanes show it, so it is a property of the kernel and not of either engine. Holding out the three largest M values and extrapolating:

held-out M predicted measured error 8192 0.987 0.930 +0.057 16384 0.993 0.911 +0.082 32768 0.997 0.875 +0.121

So eps_max is fitted to an asymptote the kernel never reaches, and a fit that has not seen large M over-predicts there by up to 12 points of efficiency.

Why this is recorded and not fixed. A decode step's M is the token count in the batch, and the corpus runs M = 1 to 2048 with 97.2% of points (1,036 of 1,066) at M <= 128. The decline begins above M ~ 4096, outside the range any evaluated deployment reaches. Scoring the same fit inside and outside the operating range:

lane range n rms mean signed vllm/0.25.0 M <= 128 (97% of corpus steps) 30 0.0585 +0.0509 vllm/0.25.0 M <= 2048 (all corpus steps) 52 0.0745 +0.0009 trtllm/1.3.0rc20 M <= 128 30 0.0474 +0.0393 trtllm/1.3.0rc20 M <= 2048 52 0.0538 +0.0040

This refuses a vLLM-lane GEMM relane. In the range that matters TRT-LLM fits better on both measures, which is consistent with §2's finding that the lanes agree to 0.4-3.6% on shared shapes — the same cuBLAS/CUTLASS kernels underneath — so the larger TRT-LLM sweep wins on determination rather than on engine. The lane rule is "fit the engine you predict" only where the engine changes the kernel, and for GEMM it does not.

Both lanes over-predict efficiency at small M (+0.039 and +0.051), which UNDER-predicts decode latency on the shapes that dominate the corpus. That is a real, quantified direction for future work, and it is a form problem: the fix is a non-monotone ramp or a small-M correction term, not a different collection.

docs.title: 7.4 What FPM could and could not adjudicate
docs.text:
FPM is the validation source in §3, but its reach is narrower than the coefficient set:

  • SWA: unusable. No FPM model carries a sliding-window node. Four of the six models in the FPM catalog have a graph in the catalog — MiniMax-M2.7 (gqa), GLM-5.2 (gqa, sparse_mla), DeepSeek-V4-Pro (gqa, mla, sparse_mla) and Kimi-K3 (kda, mla) — and none declares kind: swa; the other two (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731) have no catalog graph, so the kernel cannot price them either way. The relane in §7.1 therefore rests on held-out AISimulate folds plus provenance, with no FPM arbiter, and that is weaker evidence than a GEMM change would carry.
  • KDA: unusable for the same reason; Kimi-K3's FPM artifacts carry no KDA-node forward pass in the local snapshot.
  • GEMM: usable in principle — each of the four graphed FPM models carries dense GEMM nodes (3 on MiniMax-M2.7, 9 on GLM-5.2, 18 on DeepSeek-V4-Pro, 17 on Kimi-K3) — but the AISimulate K and M folds above already refuse the relane on the shapes the corpus runs, so no FPM run was needed to decide it. An FPM fold remains the right arbiter for a change to the ramp's FORM, which §7.3 identifies and does not attempt.

docs.title: 8. Lane provenance: every coefficient family, and every remaining borrow
docs.text: The lane rule in §2 is applied per operator. This section is the resulting census, so a reader can tell at a glance which engine's measurements each coefficient rests on, and which four are borrowed because no alternative exists.

docs.title: 8.1 The census
docs.text:
Counts in this section were taken when it was written. The current counts, generated from coefficients/ on every documentation build, are on the reference pages.

lane n share what it is nccl 498 68.8% all_gather, reduce_scatter, all_to_all, and the int8 all-reduce vllm 152 21.0% attention, GEMM, MoE imbalance, KDA, and the fp16 all-reduce descriptor 64 8.8% NVIDIA's own systems/<sku>.yaml — HBM derate, PCIe, NCCL buffers (p2p and the memory-access constant then; both since retired) none 6 0.8% host overheads, all method: assumed trtllm 2 0.3% mamba2 — borrow sglang 2 0.3% A100 MoE imbalance — borrow

NCCL is not a borrow. It is vLLM's own path for every collective except all-reduce: CustomAllreduce implements all-reduce only, and should_custom_all_gather / should_custom_reduce_scatter gate and fall through. AISimulate ships no vLLM data for those operators because there is nothing to measure. Of the 654 data-fitted coefficients, 650 (99.4%) rest on vLLM's actual execution path — 152 vLLM-lane plus 498 NCCL. The remaining four are the borrows in §8.3.

Since this census (#36, §10.5): the moe_routing_imbalance_p90 family is retired, so the A100 borrow is one entry and the vLLM lane loses seven; the descriptor rows are 48 now that hbm_constant_latency, p2p_latency and the a100_pcie duplicates are gone; and the vLLM lane gains ten entries (the Marlin ramp on h200, h100 and gb300, the V4.1 sparse rate and indexer floor on h200 and h100). The reference pages carry the current counts.

docs.title: 8.2 Per-family detail
docs.text:
set family n lanes attention attention_decode_{floor,rate} 14 vllm 0.25.0 ×10, 0.24.0 ×2, 0.14.0 ×2 attention attention_decode_*_swa 12 vllm 0.25.0 ×10, 0.24.0 ×2 attention attention_prefill_{floor,work_scale} 14 vllm 0.25.0 ×10, 0.24.0 ×2, 0.14.0 ×2 collectives all-reduce fp16 (floor, peak, transition) 69 vllm 0.24.0 ×36, 0.14.0 ×18, nccl ×15 collectives every other collective 429 nccl 2.29.2 / 2.27.3 primitives gemm_{eps_max,m_half} 52 vllm 0.27.1 ×32, 0.25.0 ×12, 0.24.0 ×6, 0.14.0 ×2 primitives moe_routing_imbalance_median 8 vllm ×7, sglang 0.5.10 ×1 (A100) — the p90 family was retired in #36 primitives gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w4a16_mxfp4_grouped 6 vllm 0.25.0 ×6 (h200, h100, gb300), §10.5 primitives gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w8a16_mxfp8, host_gather_rate_uva 6 assumed bounds (h200, h100), §10.5 primitives descriptors 48 AISimulate systems/<sku>.yaml attention attention_decode_rate_sparse_mla, attention_decode_*_block_index_scores 6 vllm 0.25.0 ×4 + 2 assumed (h200, h100; deepseek-v4.1-flash), §10.5 attention attention_decode_{launch_floor,split_floor,serial_rate,per_token,throughput_rate}_sparse_mla 10 vllm 0.25.0 ×10 (h200, h100; deepseek-v4.1-flash), §10.7 attention attention_prefill_*_sparse_mla, attention_prefill_*_block_index_scores 14 vllm 0.25.0 ×8 + 6 assumed proxy (h200, h100; deepseek-v4.1-flash), §10.6 primitives mhc_{floor,rate}_{pre,post} 8 vllm 0.25.0 ×8 (h200, h100; deepseek-v4.1-flash), §10.6 recurrent recurrent_decode_*_kda 6 vllm 0.1.dev19262 recurrent recurrent_decode_*_mamba2 2 trtllm 1.3.0rc20 host-overheads all part-wide 7 none — method: assumed host-overheads deepseek-v4.1-flash 4 eager launch assumed on h200 (end-to-end anchor) and transferred to the other eight parts (an assumed transfer), admission per token assumed (a front-end timing on an Apple M1 Max, transferred), per request not_charged 0.0 (an inference from what was timed, bounded end to end; the contracts require not_charged for a zero), §10.6

Regenerate this table rather than editing it: every count above is derivable from coefficients/ with a group-by on the family stem, and a retyped count is the defect class this registry has caught most often.

Where a part has no collection at the newest version, it uses the newest it has: L40S's attention and GEMM come from vllm/0.24.0 because 0.25.0 does not cover it, and A100's from vllm/0.14.0. The citation on each entry names the collection it was fitted on.

docs.title: 8.3 The four borrows, and why each is unavoidable
docs.text:
mamba2 (2 entries, trtllm/1.3.0rc20). mamba2_perf.parquet exists on the TRT-LLM lane and nowhere else — checked across all eight SKUs in the tree. The vLLM linear_attention collections carry gdn_perf.parquet only. A strict vLLM-only registry could not price Nemotron-3 hybrids at all. The entries remain a documented LOWER BOUND regardless of lane: the sweep has only causal_conv1d_fn and causal_conv1d_update, so the selective-scan kernel that does the rest of a Mamba2 layer is in no collection.

A100 MoE imbalance (1 entry since the p90 family was retired; 2 when written, sglang/0.5.10). A100's only vLLM MoE collection (vllm/0.14.0) contains power_law_1.01 and power_law_1.2 rows and no balanced rows at all. The coefficient is a ratio of skewed to balanced latency at identical shape, so with no balanced measurement there is no ratio to take. SGLang's sweep carries all three distributions. A100's GEMM entries DID move to the vLLM lane — that sweep is usable — so this is the narrowest possible borrow.

docs.title: 8.4 What validates what
docs.text:
The three-level separation in §3 assigns FPM the validation role, but FPM's reach is narrower than the coefficient set and it is worth being exact about where it applies.

FPM's 59 records are 41 vLLM and 18 SGLang, across five GPU families: B200 (17), GB300 (21), H200 (13), GB200 (4), B300_SXM (4). So:

  • GEMM and MoE: validatable. Every FPM model carries dense GEMM nodes, and the MoE models carry GroupedGEMM, on chips the catalog prices.
  • Attention, full and windowed: GQA and MLA are validatable; sliding window is not — no FPM model declares a kind: swa node. The SWA relane therefore rests on held-out AISimulate folds (§7.1) plus lane correctness, with no FPM arbiter.
  • KDA: the data exists and is now reachable, but one gap remains and it is not the one previously recorded here. Four Kimi-K3 artifacts are all vLLM and all on GB300, two of them on vllm/0.1.dev19262 — the same collection the kernel fit used, which is the cleanest possible pairing. An earlier revision of this section said the catalog had no gb300 chip; it has carried one since blis-catalog#23, and this registry carries 102 GB300 coefficients including the KDA pair. The dataset's own catalog index lists both artifacts as aic_fpm_forward_perf with phases: [decode, prefill], 5,266 and 4,874 rows at tep8.

What blocks the scoring now is a rank width, not a chip. The tep8 artifact is tp=8, moe_ep=8, and NCCL sweeps GB300 at 2 and 4 ranks only because a Grace-Blackwell tray is four GPUs — so all_gather, reduce_scatter and alltoall carry method: assumed 8-rank floors (§8.5) rather than measurements. All-reduce IS measured at 8 and 16 ranks, from vLLM's own custom kernel. The second artifact, vllm/0.29.0/tp8-dcp8, is moe_ep=1 / pure_tp, so it exercises no expert all-to-all and is the cleaner first cell to score.

Which MoE kernel that run used matters, and it is not stock v0.31.0's. The FPM metadata for the 0.1.dev19262/tep8 leaves records moe_quant_mode: w4a16_mxfp4 as the effective runtime identity (fpm_identity_correction, policy runtime-dtype-annotation-v1): the Kimi-K3 preview build ran its MXFP4 experts on MarlinExperts W4A16, because its CUTLASS path rejected SiTU (AISimulate collector/vllm/collect_moe.py). Stock v0.31.0 would instead select CutlassExpertsMxfp4 (W4A4) on SM100. So scoring that run needs the kernel to price Marlin W4A16 experts at the BF16 rate class, which is what gemm_*_w4a16_mxfp4_grouped on gb300 measures (§10.5). The cost model selects ramps by weight format and chip (blis-latency-kernel#44), which on gb300 is the FP4 class -- right for stock v0.31.0 -- so this entry stays unread until a deployment can state that its MoE backend is Marlin. The scoring attempt recorded on #25 also over-predicted by ~2x with the FASTER FP4 rate class, and making the KDA read free left that unchanged, so the MoE/GEMM composition is a second blocker. #41 carries the validation forward.

Note also that FPM carries no per-kernel or per-node column at all — the truth parquets hold one latency_ms per (batch_size, total_prefill_tokens, total_kv_read_tokens). "No KDA-node forward pass" describes something FPM never had for any model; the right question is only whether a Kimi-K3 whole-forward measurement exists on a chip the kernel can price, and it does. * mamba2: no FPM artifact carries a Mamba2 forward pass, and no InferenceX tier carries Nemotron-3. Unvalidatable from either direction. * A100 and L40S: absent from FPM and from InferenceX entirely. Their coefficients are fitted and shipped but carry no end-to-end check, which is stated rather than implied.

docs.title: 8.5 Rack-scale rank widths, and the one place this registry extrapolates
docs.text:
A Grace-Blackwell tray is four GPUs, so AISimulate's NCCL sweeps cover 2 and 4 ranks only on GB200-NVL72 and GB300 — against 2, 4 and 8 on every SXM part. tp=8 is an ordinary deployment on both, so three of the four collectives have no 8-rank measurement on any lane. All-reduce does: vLLM's own custom_allreduce_perf.parquet sweeps GB300 at 2, 4, 8 and 16 ranks, and since §5 already puts every fp16 all-reduce on that lane, the 8-rank figure is a first-class measurement rather than a borrow.

For the other three, all_gather, reduce_scatter and alltoall, GB300 ships 18 entries at method: assumed. This is the only extrapolation in the registry, and it is constructed to the standard cost-model-host-overheads.yaml set: dimension derived, magnitude caveated, replacement experiment named.

The model that was refuted first. Ring hop-count predicts the 4→8 floor ratio as (2·7/8)/(2·3/4) = 1.167 for all-reduce. The measured median across the seven parts swept at both widths is 1.703. Hop count is wrong by 46%, because a collective floor is dominated by per-rank synchronisation and launch cost rather than by hops. Grounding on textbook ring algebra would have under-priced these by a third; the refutation is recorded because the wrong model is the plausible one.

The model that holds. floor(n) = a + b·(n−1), with a and b fitted on each part's own measured widths {2, 4} and evaluated at n=8. Validated as a holdout on the NVLink parts that do carry 8-rank data:

operator n pred/meas median range all_reduce 14 0.987 0.953–1.041 all_gather 14 1.017 0.954–1.090 reduce_scatter 14 1.018 0.967–1.107 alltoall 14 1.128 0.737–1.294

alltoall is the stated exception and its entries say so: its floor barely grows with width (median 4→8 ratio 1.090), so a two-point linear fit amplifies noise.

The reference class excludes L40S and RTX Pro 6000, whose 8/4 rate ratios reach 2.7×–4.2×. Those parts have no NVLink, so an 8-rank group crosses a materially different fabric. GB300 is full-NVSwitch: its descriptor states inter_node_bw == intra_node_bw == 900 GB/s, so crossing a tray boundary inside the rack is not a bandwidth change at all — only the rack boundary is, and that is a 9× step to InfiniBand. Including PCIe parts would have inflated the extrapolation.

Rates are not extrapolated. The 8-rank peak and transition rates carry the part's own 4-rank measured values. A geometric decay fitted on {2,4} under-predicts the measured 8-rank rate by a median 0.84×–0.95×, and the ring-bandwidth law by 0.91×–0.94× — both biased low rather than centred, so neither is a sound estimator. Carrying the 4-rank figure gives a rate that is above the true 8-rank rate, which is an upper bound on throughput and therefore a lower bound on transfer time. That direction is stated in each entry rather than left for a reader to infer.

What replaces all 18 at once: one 8-rank GB300 NCCL sweep.

The kernel enforces the boundary. The cost model reads the measured widths from the registry per chip rather than from a constant, and a width inside the sweep range that this part was never measured at is an error naming the operator, width and chip — not a silent clamp to a narrower floor. Before that change a GB200 tp=8 group was priced at the 4-rank coefficient, understating an 8-rank all-reduce by 1.53×–1.91× across the parts measured at both widths.

docs.title: 9. The FPM mixed rows, and what they found
docs.text: §8.4 noted that FPM's reach is narrower than the coefficient set. It was also being under-used: 79.2% of FPM is MIXED prefill+decode rows (67,736 of 85,484), and none had ever been scored. scripts/score_fpm_mixed.py closes that, and the result is the largest single finding in this work.

docs.title: 9.1 What the coordinates mean, verified in AISimulate's own source
docs.text:
FPM's coordinate system is iteration_totals_balanced_v1 (crates/core/src/perfmodel/perf_database/fpm_forward.rs:59), and the totals are per-rank iteration totals, not global ones. AISimulate builds a query as

// crates/core/src/perfmodel/operators/fpm_forward.rs:203-218
FpmPhase::Prefill => vec![b, b * s as f64, b * prefix as f64],
FpmPhase::Decode   => vec![b, b / w * s as f64],

so total_prefill_tokens = batch × per_request_prefill and total_kv_read_tokens = batch × per_request_context. Dividing by batch_size to recover the per-request shape the kernel takes is therefore the correct inverse, and is what select_overlap_band.py already documents. The source warns that the round trip adds integer-division rounding, which is why the scorer medians per grid point rather than per row.

For a data-parallel cell the recorded latency is the maximum across DP ranks (collector/fpm_forward/native_artifact.py:704, expected_wall_time = max(value for _, value in wall_times)), not a mean — so a DP cell's measurement is gated by its slowest rank.

docs.title: 9.2 Six cells scored, and the error is strongly topology-dependent
docs.text:
NoOverlap edge, all mixed grid points, against the committed registry:

cell parallelism n mean abs signed over m27 pure_tp4 tp4, ep1 5,986 15.63% −13.63% 13.0% m27 tep2 tp2, ep2 5,782 20.13% −14.86% 20.8% m27 tep4 tp4, ep4 5,986 25.58% −25.24% 3.1% m27 dep2 tp1, dp2, ep2 5,383 34.58% −33.96% 2.6% m27 dep4 tp1, dp4, ep4 5,918 47.14% −46.67% 1.6% glm-5.2 tep8 tp8, ep8 5,910 49.79% −45.04% 10.5%

Every cell under-predicts, and the error spans 13% to 47% — a 3.4× range across topologies of the same model on the same chip. That is not scatter; it is a missing term that scales with parallelism.

The error is also flat across the prefill share of the batch on the tep4 cell (−25.05% below 25% prefill, −22.57% at 25–75%, −28.40% above 75%), so it is not a prefill-specific or a decode-specific defect. The whole forward pass is under-priced.

docs.title: 9.3 The mechanism: attention-DP funnels every rank's tokens into the experts
docs.text:
With attention data parallelism, all DP ranks' tokens are concatenated before expert routing, so the MoE grouped GEMM sees dp × tokens rather than one rank's share. Three independent sources agree:

  • vLLM: fused_moe/routed_experts_capturer.py:115-117 — "n == total (naive dispatch): all DP ranks' tokens are concatenated before routing". naive and allgather_reducescatter are that path, and allgather_reducescatter is vLLM's default (config/parallel.py:195).
  • AISimulate: crates/core/src/perfmodel/operators/moe.rs:287 — let num_tokens = num_tokens.saturating_mul(self.attention_dp_size.max(1)); with the comment "Attention-dp scales up the total input tokens (all dp ranks all-gather into one shared expert pool)".
  • blis-latency-kernel, at the release these cells were scored on: kernel.go:402 — routedPerRank := tokensF * float64(l.TopK) * k.localExpertShare. No DP factor. DP reaches exactly one decision, SequenceParallelMoE (internal/resolve/layout.go:106), and that rule requires tp > 1 && dp > 1 (blis-schemas rules/rules.go:196, at the same release) — so on the two dep cells, which carry tp=1, DP influences no pricing term at all.

The two dep cells are the two worst MiniMax results and they order by dp (−33.96% at dp=2, −46.67% at dp=4), which is the direction and roughly the magnitude a missing ×dp on the routed term predicts. The cost model applies that factor (moeDPFunnel in kernel/kernel.go, used by the routed term in kernel/step.go).

What this does NOT explain. glm-5.2 tep8 is dp=1 and still −45.04%, so a missing DP factor cannot be the whole account. GLM-5.2 differs from MiniMax-M2.7 in more than topology — it carries sparse_mla attention and a separate indexer GEMM — so that cell needs its own diagnosis rather than being folded into this one. Stating the limit is the point: one mechanism explains the MiniMax ordering, and a second, unidentified term is still live on GLM.

docs.title: 9.4 A committed figure this corrected
docs.text:
docs/registry/band-selection.md reports NoOverlap's signed mean as −3.44% over 219 points and calls it "nearly unbiased". Scoring every pure-decode grid point in the m27 tep4 artifact rather than the 45 the old band sweep reached gives −22.93% (1,500 points), or −19.27% restricted to batches within the scenario's declared max_num_seqs of 256 (1,048 points). FPM carries 1,557 distinct decode grid points for that cell, so the committed figure rested on under 3% of the evidence available for it, and the deficit grows with batch (−12.8% at batch 8 to −31.3% at 512) in a way a 45-point slice can miss.

The band CHOICE is unaffected — NoOverlap beats Overlap on every slice measured here, by about 7pp on the mixed rows. The claim of near-unbiasedness is withdrawn.

docs.title: 10. Sparse MLA: the byte count is the fix, and the rate is not fittable
docs.text: Commit 587c1be recorded sparse MLA as unfittable, and the kernel's new.go said sparse_mla was "deliberately NOT mapped … the registry carries no fit for it", so every layer of deepseek-v4-pro was priced as if it read the whole KV cache. Checking that against the data rather than inheriting it produced a split answer: the byte count was the defect and is now fixed in the kernel, while a per-kind rate turns out not to be identifiable from this dataset at all. Both halves are recorded because the negative one is the more useful.

docs.title: 10.1 The table that is not a module measurement
docs.text:
The sparse_attention family ships thirteen tables per part. Twelve floor between 37.7 µs and 1,186 µs on h200 — at or above the 66.2 µs it costs to read the csa4_moe layer's 317.5 MB of projections at 4.80 TB/s, which the catalog's graph prices as nine separate GEMM nodes. Those are module measurements, and fitting a kernel coefficient from one is the defect scripts/correct_mla_floor.py had to undo (§3, sixth entry).

One is not: dsv4_hca_attn_module_perf floors at 9.6 µs on the FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV4 lane — below this part's 13.5 µs GQA attention floor and 7× below the projection read. 35,262 rows across all six NVIDIA parts, and uniquely in the family a compress_ratio column.

docs.title: 10.2 The byte count, chosen by search rather than assumed
docs.text:
Candidate forms were grid-searched against (floor, rate) on three parts. The discriminator is whether the optimum is interior: a form that under-counts bytes forces the rate to the grid ceiling, which is how a wrong byte count announces itself.

form h200 error rate as fraction of peak full context — the old fallback 1.698 1.00 — clamped on every part topk=128 only 1.309 0.07 topk=128 + (step−128)/128 1.301 0.08 topk=1024 + (step−1024)/4 1.483 1.00 — clamped

The winner is exactly the geometry the catalog declares for csa128_moe (window: 128, compress_ratio: 128) — resolved from the catalog, not tuned. The full-context form clamping at 1.00 of datasheet peak on all three parts is the quantitative statement that the old fallback could not describe this kernel: it needed a physically impossible bandwidth to cover the measured time.

The physics is directly visible. At batch 1 on h200 latency is flat at 9.8–13.7 µs from step 0 to 16,384 and reaches only 30.6 µs at step 1,048,575 — a 1 M-token context costs about as much as a 16 K one.

docs.title: 10.3 Why a per-kind rate is NOT fittable, which is the finding
docs.text:
A rate was fitted — 0.083–0.111 of datasheet peak across six parts, errors 1.30×–1.36× with head and tail balanced — and then withdrawn, because the end-to-end check refused it:

configuration overall TPOT deepseek-v4-pro TPOT neither (full context, part-wide rate) 14.98 % 10.42 % sparse byte count only 15.04 % 8.72 % sparse byte count + sparse rate 14.95 % 14.36 %

The byte count earns 1.7 points on the affected model. The rate costs 5.6.

The mechanism is not noise, and it is specific. deepseek-v4-pro alternates two sparse geometries — 30 csa128_moe layers (window 128, ratio 128) and 30 csa4_moe layers (index_topk 1024, ratio 4) — whose selected-token counts differ by 32× at a 1 M context (8,319 against 262,912). The fitted rate came from dsv4_hca_attn_module_perf, which states compress_ratio: 128 on every row, so it describes csa128_moe alone. Charging it to all 60 layers applies a rate fitted on the small read to the large one.

And this dataset cannot supply the missing half. compress_ratio: 4 appears only in the dsv4_csa_* tables, and every one of those is a module measurement (floors 61.4–80.6 µs). Fitting a csa4_moe rate from them would re-import the projection double-charge. A rate covering half a model's layers is not a coefficient — it is a bias with a provenance string, so no part-wide attention_decode_rate_sparse_mla ships. (One ships scoped to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on h200, whose every sparse layer is inside the measured range; §10.5 says why that is a different question.)

scripts/fit_attention_sparse_mla.py is kept as a negative result, the way fit_attention_mla.py and probe_moe_roofline.py are: the fit is clean, physical, and wrong for this cost model, and deleting it would leave the next person to re-derive that.

docs.title: 10.4 What shipped instead
docs.text:
The fix is in the kernel, not the registry, and it needs no fitted constant: selectedKVTokens bounds a sparse layer's decode read per layer and per request from the catalog's own index_topk, window and compress_ratio. Sparse layers keep the part-wide measured floor and rate, now charged against the right number of bytes.

Per-request rather than batch-wide because min(sum) ≠ sum(min): a batch holding one request below the top-k and one far above it gets both wrong if the bound is applied to the aggregate. Per-layer because the two geometries above differ by 32×.

No schema change was needed: the model graph already carried index_topk and compress_ratio (blis-schemas v0.2.0); the kernel's layer plan was not reading them.

The generalizable point, and it is the same one §3 makes from the other direction: a coefficient can be measurable and still not be identifiable for the thing it will be charged against. Here the quantity was measured cleanly on one of two layer geometries, and only the end-to-end check could tell that this made it unusable.

docs.title: 10.5 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on H200: what vLLM v0.31.0 runs, and what is measured of it
docs.text:
inference-sim/blis-registry#37, #38 and #39 asked for the coefficients the kernels vLLM v0.31.0 runs for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SM90 need. Every kernel identity below is read from the v0.31.0 tag (db9527a4); every number is written by scripts/fit_deepseek_v41_h200.py or scripts/fit_marlin_grouped_ramp.py, both with --check.

No vLLM 0.31 sweep exists, so the timed path was compared instead. AISimulate's newest vLLM collection for h200 is vllm/0.25.0. For each kernel used here, the source the two tags build was diffed, and what the 0.25.0 timing does and does not contain is stated:

what v0.25.0 → v0.31.0 effect on the fit FlashMLA SM90 sparse decode (flash_mla_with_kvcache) vllm-project/FlashMLA a6ec2ba → 0eee43b: namespace, include paths, MODEL1 → V4; the 584 B BYTES_PER_TOKEN assert unchanged none FlashMLA split-KV combine, same call grid (b, s_q, h) → (b·s_q, 1, h); 192/224/256-split cases added inert at one query token per request; the new cases are reached only past 160 splits FlashMLA host API rewritten; the split workspace is skipped for unsplit requests (0397728d) host-side, not in the device time top-k → cache-slot translation V4.1 launches compute_global_topk_indices_and_lens on every compressed (ratio 1 or 2) decode layer (nvidia/flashmla.py:181-188, under if not swa_only); the 0.25.0 ratio-128 rows take indices from metadata a known gap: one small Triton launch per layer the rate does not price DeepGEMM fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM a6b593d → vllm-project/DeepGEMM e1f418c (v0.31.0 builds vLLM's fork): renames; bounds handling for zero-length contexts and block-table rows past a request's pages none Marlin MoE template (marlin_moe_wna16) the runtime act-order path removed (#54809), compile-time dead for MXFP4's group-32 instantiation none Marlin MoE Python (fused_moe/experts/marlin_moe.py) 10 commits; #48144 sets the M used for block-size selection under EP to ceil(M · local / global experts) inert at ep 1, where the ramp is fitted; the 0.25.0 rows at ep > 1 may not describe v0.31.0 wherever it changes the chosen block size

What ships.

entry scope method value from attention_decode_rate_sparse_mla h200, deepseek-v4.1-flash measured 1,123,200 B/µs (0.234 of peak), floor inherited (13.5 µs) dsv4_hca_attn_module_perf, V4-Flash rows: the h64 FlashMLA instance and 584 B record V4.1 runs attention_decode_floor_block_index_scores h200, deepseek-v4.1-flash measured 4.3 µs dsv4_paged_mqa_logits_module_perf, the kernel itself under CUDA graphs attention_decode_rate_block_index_scores h200, deepseek-v4.1-flash assumed 3,840,000 B/µs, NVIDIA's empirical HBM rate (BwPeak × hbm_derate), not a bound see below gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w4a16_mxfp4_grouped h200, gb300 measured 0.245 / 26 (h200), 0.114 / 55 (gb300), of the BF16 peak vLLM's MarlinExperts MXFP4 rows, fitted under the kernel's routed-term composition. On gb300 it applies only where the MoE backend is Marlin W4A16 (the Kimi-K3 preview build FPM measured), not to stock v0.31.0 gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w8a16_mxfp8 h200 assumed the BF16 envelope: an upper bound on the asymptote; the knee is not a bound no dense Marlin sweep exists on any part gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w8a16_mxfp8 h200 transferred the part's own measured Marlin grouped pair (0.245 / 26), which the lookup prefers to the assumed bound above (rank 3 against 7). h100's pair (0.282 / 15) is a candidate, not in this registry: it has no held-out unit, so the bound prices h100 no dense Marlin sweep exists on any part; unkeyed, see reproducing-coefficients host_gather_rate_uva h200 assumed 57,764 B/µs: the PCIe 5.0 raw rate × 128/130 line code × 264/288 no host-gather measurement exists

On H100 the same six entries ship, each fitted from H100's own rows. H100 SXM is the same GH100 die and SM90 kernels as H200 with 0.70× its HBM (3.35 against 4.8 TB/s), and AISimulate's h100_sxm carries the same three tables. The writers fit every part they list from that part's sweep, catalog descriptor and committed siblings; no h200 number enters an h100 entry.

entry h100 value h200 value fit attention_decode_rate_sparse_mla 1,105,500 B/µs (0.330 of peak), floor inherited (14.5 µs) 1,123,200 (0.234) 1.198x, signed 1.057, n = 207; held out ≥ 5 blocks 1.175x (signed 0.853, n = 16); at 10 blocks 1.069x (n = 4) attention_decode_floor_block_index_scores 4.9 µs 4.3 1.086x, n = 414; 246 floor-dominated points 1.067x; per checkpoint 4.95 / 4.90 attention_decode_rate_block_index_scores 2,680,000 B/µs, BwPeak × hbm_derate (3.35 × 0.8) 3,840,000 assumed; the sweep's slope is 6.44 TB/s-equivalent, 1.92× H100's peak gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w4a16_mxfp4_grouped 0.282 / 15 0.245 / 26 1.140x, signed 1.039, n = 27; int4 holdout 1.161x, signed 1.068 gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w8a16_mxfp8 1.0 / 170, H100's BF16 envelope 0.992 / 110 assumed (h200 also carries a transferred pair above it; h100's is a non-selected candidate) host_gather_rate_uva 57,764 B/µs, H100's own host_link_bandwidth × 128/130 × 264/288 57,764 assumed

Neither fitted pair scales with bandwidth, and the rows say so directly. On the 207 FlashMLA rows both parts measure, H100 latency is a median 1.05× H200's (1.13× over the slowest tenth), where an HBM-bound read would be 1.43×; on the 27 Marlin token counts it is 0.98–1.06×. So the sparse rate is close to H200's (0.98×) and a larger fraction of H100's peak: at reads of at most 10 blocks per request it is a cost per byte, not a bandwidth, and must not be rescaled between parts by BwPeak. The Marlin ramp differs from H200's because its memory half is charged at H100's lower BwPeak × hbm_derate, and the SM half carries what is left; the pair holds only with that part's own memory half. The sparse rate's batch bias has the same shape on H100 (signed 1.02 at batch 1, 1.44 at 128, 0.59 at 1,024), and the per-request and occupancy forms again leave it (1.186x, 1.179x). The pinned 14.5 µs floor over-prices batch-1 one-block reads (10.1–10.6 µs) by 37–44%.

No end-to-end check is possible on H100. No forward-pass dataset carries DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on h100 under any engine, and the h200 rows FPM does carry are SGLang (next paragraph), so nothing arbitrates the h100 entries either; each rationale says so.

The sparse rate's error depends on batch, and V4.1 runs where the table has no rows. The overall 1.182x hides a batch-dependent bias. Signed, predicted over measured, by batch:

batch 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 512 1024 signed 0.99 1.04 1.07 1.09 1.08 1.05 1.25 1.45 1.10 0.80 0.65
  • Not a missing term this form can carry. A per-request term, floor + c · batch + bytes / rate (1.179x), and an occupancy form, floor + a · ceil(batch · blocks / P) with P fitted at 64 (1.173x), leave the same pattern, so it is batch-dependent scheduling inside the call. The writer fits and prints both.
  • Inside the measured range on the block axis only. V4.1 reads at most 640 tokens per query, 10 FlashMLA blocks (2 window + 8 top-k), inside the 1–130 the table covers. But the sweep's batch × context ≤ 1 M grid pairs 10 blocks only with batch ≤ 8, while V4.1 reads 10 blocks at any context past about 1k tokens, at whatever batch it serves. Above batch 8 the rate's error is what the table says about neighbouring cells: at batch 64 and up, 10–45% slow or 20–35% fast.
  • The holdout is in the small-batch region too. Trained on requests of at most 3 blocks and tested on 5 or more, it predicts 1.210x, signed 0.83 — but all 16 held-out rows are at batch ≤ 16.

The pinned floor over-prices the shortest reads. The floor is this part's 13.5 µs part-wide attention floor, which the kernel inherits for a kind with a rate and no floor. Batch-1 rows of at most one block measure 9.8–11.8 µs, so pinning costs 14–38% there. A free floor lands at 13.3 µs (1.181x against 1.182x) only because a linear form cannot follow the step between one and two blocks. On V4.1 a read of one block occurs on the window-only layers (0, 1, and the DSpark drafts) at contexts up to 64 tokens, and on a ratio-2 layer at context 1, where the indexer emits min((pos + 1) // ratio, topk) = 0 compressed tokens; past that every compressed layer reads at least two blocks.

Why a sparse rate ships for V4.1 when §10.3 withdrew one for V4-Pro. The withdrawn rate was fitted on Pro's 128-head rows — the h128 instance, which Pro runs only below TP 2, since FlashMLA pads n_local_heads — and was to be charged against the kernel's selection rule for Pro's csa4 layers: up to 262,912 tokens at a 1 M context, outside every measured row on the block axis (vLLM itself reads far less there; blis-latency-kernel#32). Every V4.1 sparse read is on the h64 instance at every TP width and inside the block axis. The entry is scoped to this model, so no other deployment moves.

Why the indexer's rate is assumed when its floor is measured. The collector gives every query row one block table, so the unique key footprint is at most 34.6 MB, and the fitted throughput, 5.35 TB/s-equivalent, exceeds the 4.8 TB/s HBM peak — impossible from HBM, and consistent with the shared keys being served from cache. A fit of that slope would be clean and wrong in the §3 sense. The floor is a launch cost: the 238 points whose work term is under 5% of it identify it at 1.050x, and each checkpoint alone gives 4.29 and 4.28 µs. In serving each request's keys are its own, read at ceil(context / ratio) × 132 B; V4.1's ratios are 1 and 2, so the scan grows with context while the attention it feeds does not. The committed rate is NVIDIA's empirical HBM fraction (BwPeak × hbm_derate), not a bound: the real rate cannot exceed BwPeak, so it can be pessimistic by at most 1.25x (scan time over-priced), while how optimistic it can be is not bounded. The writer refuses to keep assuming it if a future sweep's throughput stops exceeding the HBM peak.

Why the Marlin ramp is fitted in the kernel's composition, and what it is coupled to. A weight-only GEMM is two costs, a BF16 mma.sync compute and a narrow weight read. The kernel sums them for the routed term, and fitting the ramp as what remains after the kernel's own memory half is the only way it composes back to the measurement. That couples it to the cost model's routed term as blis-latency-kernel#44 (483f6aa) implements it:

  • compute and memory summed, the ramp evaluated at the step's token count, compute at the BF16 peak, memory as ExpertsTouched experts' stored bytes at BwPeak × hbm_derate, imbalance and SM derate 1;
  • FLOPs the rank's own, the intermediate width divided by tp, which #44 applies on this ramp;
  • no Marlin padding: #44 also scales routed FLOPs and bytes by Marlin's round-up of inter / tp to a multiple of 128 (V4.1 at TP8: 288 → 384). Fitted at tp 1, where that pad is 1, the fit has not checked it; it is the consumer's addition;
  • stored bytes per weight as model.StoredBytes in contracts/spec/model gives them for MXFP4, 0.5 + 1/32, which #44 charges. At payload-only bytes (0.5, what blis-latency-kernel e9cf217 charged) the fit would be 0.240 / 28 on h200, 0.114 / 58 on gb300.

A change to any of those — sum versus max, the ramp's argument, the byte count — needs a refit. The fit holds out on vLLM's int4 Marlin MoE, a different geometry and weight type: 1.196x on h200 and 1.266x on gb300. Its error grows with expert and tensor parallelism; the committed BF16 ramp does the same on BF16 Triton experts (on h200, 2.83x at ep 8 and 8.33x at ep 32, printed by the writer's form check), so that growth is a property of the routed-term form — though #48144 above means the 0.25.0 ep > 1 rows may not be v0.31.0's.

For scale: blis-latency-kernel e9cf217, before #44, priced MXFP4 experts on H200 at the FP8 peak with the FP8 ramp. That is 1,456 TFLOPS effective where Marlin sustains about 242.

What does not ship, and why.

  • A ramp for CutlassExpertsMxfp4, what stock v0.31.0 runs for compressed-tensors MXFP4 experts on Blackwell. AISimulate carries no such rows on any Blackwell part.
  • Prefill pairs for either kernel. No kernel-level table carries V4.1's prefill path (flash_mla_sparse_fwd over a gathered compressed region, fp8_fp4_mqa_logits), and the kernel has no per-kind prefill name to read one with.
  • SGLang's dsv41_module_perf (h200). It is eager, a module timing (MQALayer.forward with projections), at batch ≤ 3 and context ≤ 2,049, and flat at 0.8–2.0 ms. That is launch-bound, not a kernel rate.

No end-to-end check exists for vLLM, and that is stated rather than waived. At FPM revision 03e006de, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on h200, b200, b300, gb200 and gb300 is measured under SGLang only -- another engine, another MoE kernel (w4a16_mxfp4_humming on h200) and another checkpoint revision (fb2764a5 against the catalog's 52544481). The only vLLM V4.1 leaf is a historical GB200 dev build labelled "comparator". So FPM cannot be the arbiter §3 requires for V4.1's vLLM pricing; an earlier version of this section said it could. blis-registry#42 stays open with no arbiter until a vLLM V4.1 forward-pass measurement exists. Separately, the kernel before blis-latency-kernel#44 could not price the model: it refused the fp8_ds_mla cache (#36), charged 20,480 KV bytes per token against roughly 1,790 (#30), dropped the 128-token window from the sparse read (#32) and did not pad FlashMLA's heads (#39). #44 closes all four. Three consumer-contract points go with the entries, each stated in them:

  • Multi-token decode. The sparse rate was fitted at one query token per request. Under DSpark speculation a request decodes 1 + num_spec_tokens query tokens, and FlashMLA treats each as its own query; how much of that read the tokens of one request share is unmeasured. #44 charges the read per query row and records that as an assumption (sparse_read_per_query), which is what this entry asks of a consumer.
  • Routed FLOPs under pure TP. This ramp's FLOPs are each rank's own (inter / tp). #44 divides routed FLOPs by tp on the weight-only Marlin ramps, as this fit requires, and keeps its documented over-charge on the native ramps, where it cancels a measured error; blis-latency-kernel#47 tracks removing it there. A consumer that charged this ramp the whole expert would price its compute half tp times too slow.
  • gb300's Marlin ramp stays unread while ramps are chosen by format and chip, which on gb300 is the FP4 class — right for stock v0.31.0. It is for scoring the Kimi-K3 preview build's FPM run, for blis-registry#41 (the Kimi-K3/GB300 FPM check of the KDA pair).

Every V4.1 attention read in the catalog's graph (blis-catalog 0.3.0) is sparse_mla, the window-only layers (0, 1, and the DSpark drafts at a 133-token window) included, all inside the block axis above.

docs.title: 10.6 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash prefill attention, prefill indexer, mHC and host terms
docs.text:
Before these entries the kernel priced three V4.1 operators with numbers fitted on a different kernel or with none: the sparse-MLA PREFILL attention and the indexer's prefill logits with the generic full-attention prefill pair (attention_prefill_floor / attention_prefill_work_scale, fitted on context_attention_perf), and mHC as Elementwise bytes at the HBM rate with no floor -- 0.07 ms a one-token decode step against 1.05 ms measured, one of the two terms behind V4.1's 19-30% fast low-load ITL. Every number below is written by scripts/fit_deepseek_v41_prefill.py or scripts/fit_deepseek_v41_host.py, both with --check; each part is fitted from its own rows. The per-call forms are stated in each entry's rationale.

entry (scope: h200 / h100, deepseek-v4.1-flash) method h200 h100 fit (h200) attention_prefill_{floor,per_request,per_token,rate}_sparse_mla measured 14.8 µs, 1.323 µs, 0.049 µs, 3,159,685 B/µs 15.5, 1.325, 0.0571, 3,509,505 1.067x, signed 1.003, n = 1,642 (not V4.1's operating point: signed 0.81 at 10 blocks); held out on blocks 1.137x (signed 0.91), on chunk length 1.036x attention_prefill_{floor,per_token,rate}_block_index_scores assumed (proxy kernel) 4.1 µs, 0.00466 µs, 7,298,637 B/µs 4.7, 0.00441, 7,364,876 1.066x, signed 0.969, n = 3,504; held out on context 1.054x, on rows 1.142x mhc_{floor,rate}_pre measured 8.9 µs, 1,799,384 B/µs 9.3, 1,325,488 1.052x, n = 70; across hidden 1.103x / 1.073x mhc_{floor,rate}_post measured 3.0 µs, 1,850,611 B/µs 3.1, 1,306,352 1.091x, n = 70; across hidden 1.178x / 1.109x

Sparse-MLA prefill is fitted on the kernel table's prefill rows, in four terms. dsv4_hca_attn_module_perf times forward_mqa alone; its isl > 1 rows run the prefill branch (SWA and compressed gather, index combine, flash_mla_sparse_fwd). A floor plus a work rate over the decode fit's block-and-record count gives 1.390x with a strong batch bias (signed 0.15 at batch 1,024); a per-request and a per-query-token term remove it (1.067x, every batch within 0.96-1.05 signed). The per-token term, 0.049 µs, is the cost of a query's own traffic -- 64 padded heads of 512 BF16 in and out -- at about the part's empirical HBM rate. The fit uses only rows reading at most V4.1's 10 blocks a query. Its weak point is V4.1's operating point: the only 10-block rows are short chunks at step 65,536, under-priced 1.31x (signed 0.81), and long chunks at 10 blocks are not in the table; long-chunk rows at 11-67 blocks extrapolate at 1.05x. So the 1.067x headline is not V4.1's error. It is dominated by the rows V4.1 does not run: 980 of the 1,642 rows are at 3 blocks, 20 at 10 and none at 8-9. At V4.1's read the evidence is signed 0.81 in sample (under-priced) and, trained on fewer blocks, signed 0.91 held out on 7-10 blocks; the honest statement of this entry's error at V4.1's operating point is "about 10-20% fast, from 71 rows", not 1.067x.

These entries ship without the end-to-end check §3 and the evidence page ask for, as an explicit exception. No vLLM forward-pass measurement of V4.1 exists on any part (§10.5: FPM's V4.1 rows are SGLang), so the rule cannot be met by waiting for the data on hand; the alternative is to keep pricing V4.1 with entries fitted on other kernels, which is the known larger error. Each entry therefore says it has no arbiter, and blis-registry#42 stays open until a vLLM V4.1 forward-pass measurement exists. The SM90 sparse prefill device code is unchanged between the FlashMLA pins of vLLM 0.25.0 and 0.31.0 (renames only). V4.1's ratio-1/2 layers gather their whole compressed stream before the kernel; the ratio-128 rows hold that gather only at 1/128 of the context, so it stays with the catalog's prefill_dequant_gather node.

The indexer's prefill is a proxy, and is labelled so. vLLM v0.31.0's prefill indexer runs DeepGEMM's ragged fp8_fp4_mqa_logits; the entries are fitted on the paged fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits at prefill shapes. Unlike decode, the sweep's shared block table is representative here (every query row of a request reads the same keys), and the fitted throughput is compute-like (906 TFLOPS at 64 heads). The 32-head V4.1 indexer is scaled linearly from 64, an assumption. The ragged kernel is measured, on another lane: SGLang 0.5.14's glm5_mqa_logits_module_perf times deep_gemm.fp8_mqa_logits at GLM-5's indexer geometry -- 32 index heads x 128, FP8 keys, ratio 1, V4.1's head count. Evaluated as the kernel charges it, the proxy is 1.50x there, signed 0.93 (h200) and 0.90 (h100); signed 0.89 / 0.82 on long chunks over long prefixes and 1.18 / 1.09 at V4.1's 8,192-token chunk. An earlier review read the table's num_heads (GLM-5's 64 attention heads) as index heads and found the proxy over-pricing by 1.4-1.7x; at the config's 32 it does not. The ragged rows are not fitted because the lane decision is open: SGLang 0.5.14 calls upstream DeepGEMM's fp8_mqa_logits, vLLM v0.31.0 its fork's fp8_fp4_mqa_logits on the FP8 path, and the two pins' device code has not been compared. fit_deepseek_v41_prefill.py prints the comparison and each rationale states it.

mHC is measured per site and interpolated by bytes. mhc_module_perf times TileLang mhc_pre and mhc_post (two sites a row) at hidden 4096 and 7168; W = tokens x hidden x 8 B carries the hidden size, so one floor and rate per component fit both, and each hidden size predicted from the other lands within 1.06-1.18x. The pre includes the TF32 prenorm GEMM, so the catalog's hc_*_fn GEMM must not also be charged. On SM90 v0.31.0 runs the fused delayed post+pre, which above 32 tokens is the same two kernels and at <= 32 folds the post into the GEMM -- so at decode sizes the pair is an upper bound by about one launch.

Two terms were looked for and do not ship. Routed MoE at V4.1's geometry: no vLLM collection holds a hidden 5120 / inter 2304 / 384-expert / top-6 W4A16 row on h200 or h100. The only rows at that geometry are SGLang dev-1aa0e962 (flashinfer_cutlass at moe_tp 2, mxfp4_humming at moe_tp 4, ep 1, 15 token counts each) -- other kernels and another sharding than vLLM v0.31.0's Marlin at EP8 -- so the Kimi-K3-geometry Marlin ramp stays, with its evidence class. The compressor: no table isolates it; the csa/hca context-module tables time the whole attention module, projections included, and a residual from them would be a module-derived term of the kind §10.1 rejects. It stays at the catalog's bytes.

Host terms. host_launch_eager_per_kernel (92.87 µs, assumed) is V4.1's per-launch Python dispatch in an eager (cudagraph NONE) step -- vLLM v0.31.0 cannot torch.compile this model, so NONE is plain eager PyTorch. It is backed out of an internal enforce-eager H200 serving run of the same model (ITL flat at 93.8-101.6 ms from c1 to c64). The run's report is not redistributed: validator/testdata/anchors/v41_h200_enforce_eager_anchor.json holds only what the fit needs -- the plateau's levels, median, minimum and maximum ITL, the setup and the report's sha256 -- and --check re-derives it from a local copy of the report when V41_EAGER_ANCHOR_REPORT names one, and checks its internal consistency otherwise. The division is by the KERNEL's own launch count and device time for that step, a recorded input: v41_kernel_eager_basis.json, written by --record-device from diagnosis/kdevice (public kernel API) with clean kernel, registry and catalog commits. --check refuses a basis recorded for another anchor, scenario, host composition or step type: the anchor is a decode step, so the count must be the decode-only 972 (a step with a prefill row also launches the graph's 46 phase: prefill gathers, 1,018; kernel 993ddeb used 1,018 on every step, which gave 89.4 µs). The composition is additive, as the kernel's is: step = launches x (eager + dispatch) + device, so e = (ITL - device) / launches - host_launch_per_kernel = (96.56 - 3.18 ms) / 972 - 3.2 µs = 92.87 µs. A launch-overlap form, step ~ max(launches, device) (vLLM enqueues eager kernels asynchronously), was tried in the kernel and gave 96.14 µs here, and was REJECTED: it does not reproduce the H200 DSpark arm's capture-ceiling collapse at c32, whose measured throughput the additive form matches (blis-latency-kernel commit 07ed424, TestTheEagerDecodeAnchorIsAdditive, which pins the constant at 92.75-93.7 µs). The basis records the composition and --check refuses any other. The committed basis is kernel 07ed424 (972 launches, 3.18 ms with the mHC entries). The constant is valid only with the basis and the composition it was divided by. It is derived on H200 nodes only: the h200 entry is assumed (backed out of the anchor), and the other eight parts, h100 included, carry it as a separate transferred entry (transferred_from: hardware=h200,...). That transfer is an ASSUMPTION about host CPU and driver launch cost, not a derivation; an H100 enforce-eager ITL anchor (same model, TP8, no speculation, c1-c64) would replace it. The host set's coverage rule is checked per name and model across entries, so the split is allowed. host_admission_per_token (2.67 µs, assumed) is a timing of vLLM v0.31.0's own V4.1 front end -- render, tokenize, block hash -- taken on the diagnosis workstation (Apple M1 Max, one Python thread) with synthetic text. No part it is scoped to matches that host, so on every part it is an assumed transfer of the measurement, labelled as the eager copy is; the same timing on the serving node's CPU would replace it. And host_admission_per_request is 0.0, not_charged only because the contracts require that method for a zero value: what was timed has no fixed term above noise, but the bench does not time HTTP handling, validation, the IPC to EngineCore or scheduler admission, so the zero is an inference bounded only end to end (an 8,030-token c1 TTFT of 37.15 ms in total), not a structural zero. These two model-scoped entries sit after their part-wide namesakes in the same set, the one arrangement test_a_model_scoped_entry_never_shadows_a_part_wide_one allows: last-in-file-order and scoped-wins resolve it the same way.

docs.title: 10.7 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode: a two-branch FlashMLA form, and what stays assumed
docs.text:
The single decode rate (§10.5) is 1.18-1.20x with a batch bias it cannot carry: signed 1.45-1.54 at batch 128 and 0.59-0.80 at 1,024. The FlashMLA decode rows show two regimes. At small batch the call is latency-bound and flat in batch to about 128 rows: one block costs about 10.2 µs (h200) / 10.4 µs (h100), any read of two or more blocks adds about 3.5 µs at once (the split-KV combine launch), then 0.2-0.3 µs a block. At large batch it is linear in rows through the origin: one cost per query row and one per block read. So scripts/fit_deepseek_v41_decode.py fits, per part, on the rows of at most V4.1's 10 blocks:

t = max(launch_floor + split_floor x [B > 1] + B x 37,376 B / serial_rate,
        sum over query rows (per_token + blocks x 37,376 B / throughput_rate))
part launch floor split serial rate per token throughput rate fit held out rows ≤ 256 → ≥ 512 held out blocks ≤ 4 → ≥ 6 h200 10.0 µs 3.1 µs 115,005 B/µs 0.05437 µs 1.30 TB/s 1.061x (single rate 1.176x) 1.038x (single rate 1.375x) 1.059x h100 10.3 µs 3.6 µs 145,351 B/µs 0.06567 µs 1.27 TB/s 1.060x (single rate 1.193x) 1.028x (single rate 1.502x) 1.058x

The per-token term lands near the prefill fit's own (0.049 / 0.057 µs), an independent check that it is each row's query and output traffic. The weakness is stated in each entry: the throughput branch is identified only by the batch ≥ 256 rows, which are at 1-3 blocks. Trained on rows ≤ 64 the form predicts ≥ 128 at 1.8-1.9x, worse than the single rate (1.3x), because no training row reaches that branch. At 10 blocks the throughput branch binds above about 47 query rows per rank, a region the sweep's batch x context ≤ 1M grid never measures; there the per-block cost is extrapolated from 1-3 blocks, as the single rate's is. Batches 16-64 at 4+ blocks are under-priced (signed 0.83-0.93).

The names are new. attention_decode_floor_sparse_mla is deliberately not used: the kernel reads that name today as the floor of the single-rate pair, which was fitted over the inherited part-wide floor, and would silently re-price it. The kernel uses the form only when all five resolve.

What stays assumed, and why.

  • The indexer's decode scan rate (attention_decode_rate_block_index_scores). Both kernel-level sweeps of fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits -- vLLM 0.24.0/0.25.0 and SGLang 0.5.14 -- give every query row one shared block table, and none flushes L2. The largest unique footprint, one request at a 1M context, is 34.6 MB, inside the 50 MB L2, and its implied throughput is 7.2 TB/s-equivalent on h100 (above the 3.35 TB/s HBM peak) even at batch 1. No row reads its keys from HBM, so no row identifies the HBM-bound scan V4.1 runs in serving, where it is the one decode term that grows with context (ratio 1 and 2 over all 40 layers' index sources). Its per-row term is identified (about 0.006-0.01 µs a row at 64 heads, past 256 rows) but is under 3 µs a layer at V4.1's batches and is not shipped.
  • The decode top-k. vLLM v0.31.0 runs cooperative_topk up to 64 rows and persistent_topk beyond (indexer_topk.py, index_topk 512 on SM90). AISimulate times only SGLang's topk_transform_512 (dsv4_csa_topk_calib_perf) and its GLM-5 fused variant, different kernels with mode switches visible in the rows (0 µs, then a 48-85 µs plateau, then ~10 µs past 128k). Nothing measures vLLM's kernels, and the catalog keeps pricing the logits write and top-k read as index_logits_topk bytes.
  • compute_global_topk_indices_and_lens and V4.1's candidate select/mask: unmeasured.
  • Host and launch terms. AISimulate carries no host, launch or graph-replay rows on any part; every operator row is a device timing under CUDA-graph replay. The collective floors on h100 and h200 are already measured (NCCL and vLLM custom all-reduce), so they are not among the assumed terms. The only public timing of an engine's Python path found is FPM's GLM-5.3-Flash vLLM 0.31.0 fidelity pairs on GB300 (next paragraph); nothing times graph replay or eager launch on Hopper.

Held-out evidence for a per-request host term, not used to fit anything. Each of FPM's five GLM-5.3-Flash vLLM 0.31.0 GB300 leaves (FP8 TP2/TP4, NVFP4 TP1/TP2/TP4, checkpoint eb9eb208, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE, async scheduling off) ships source-fidelity.json, pairing each held-out point's FPM step time with a "clean" timer that excludes schedule(), the scheduler-output send and update_from_output. Re-derived here from the five files: an OLS of decode (FPM - clean) on batch over 77 points a leaf gives 20.4, 24.9, 26.4, 27.6 and 32.6 µs per request (intercepts 16-282 µs); the SGLang 0.5.20 control leaf gives -1.2. It does not hold at small batch: fitted on batch ≤ 8 alone the slopes range from -21 to +33 µs, and the residual at batch ≥ 16 is up to 1 ms, so the per-request reading rests on batch 16-32. Caveats: Grace (Arm) hosts, FPM and clean are separate runs, batch ≤ 32, and the clean timer's boundary is described only in words. It is the first in-version public timing of a per-request scheduler cost, and it agrees in magnitude with fit_host_step_per_request.py's form; it is recorded as held-out evidence for that term on gb300 and moves no value.

docs.title: 11. Memory occupancy: what composes, and where each term comes from
docs.text: cost-model-memory.yaml exists because a consumer was carrying three per-rank memory magnitudes as constants in its own source — CUDA-graph capture at 512 MiB, collective buffers at 392 MiB, activation scratch at "a few live buffers" (×4) — where no provenance readout could see them (inference-sim/blis-registry#33). They set how many sequences fit, so they are not soft numbers.

docs.title: 11.1 The composition, taken from NVIDIA's capacity path
docs.text:
AISimulate's KV-capacity estimate (aisimulate_core/sdk/memory.py) charges, per rank and outside the KV budget:

weights + activation + nccl_communicator_bytes_<N>rank + engine_workspace_bytes
        + cudagraph_capture_bytes_<mode>

Every term adds. Two questions the consumer could not answer from its side are settled by the source rather than by preference:

  • nccl_communicator_bytes_<N>rank is the whole collective-buffer reservation. base_backend.py sums nccl_mem and other_mem; neither contains the other.
  • engine_workspace_bytes (misc.other_mem) does not include CUDA-graph capture. This registry's own rationale previously said it did; AISimulate annotates other_mem as "excludes CUDA graph reservation" (support/config_profile.py) and takes the graph reservation as a separate argument (capacity.py, cuda_graph_reserved_bytes). Adding a capture term on top therefore does not double-count. The rationale is corrected in emit_primitives.py and in all nine committed entries.

docs.title: 11.2 Activation scratch — vendor_spec, NVIDIA's table
docs.text:
activation = max(activation_buffer_count_<family>_<N>rank · max_num_batched_tokens · h · 2,
                 activation_scratch_floor_bytes)

The multiple is AISimulate's ACTIVATION_COEFFICIENTS, which the vLLM backend reuses from TRT-LLM's; emit_memory.py reads it from the source with ast and refuses if vLLM stops aliasing it. Two rows are registered because the kernel can tell only whether a model routes to experts: dense (the LLAMA row, 11 / 6.5 / 5 / 5 at 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 ranks) and MoE (22 / 13 / 10 / 10). h is num_attention_heads × head_dim, equal to hidden_size unless a config declares a different head_dim; N is min(tp, 8).

Three scoping decisions, each a finding rather than a convenience:

  • The 2 is the model dtype, not the served one. The issue proposed sizing scratch at the served width (1 byte for fp8). vLLM's quantized linears return out_dtype=x.dtype (vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/cutlass.py): the fp8 operand is a transient copy, and the residual stream stays bf16. Halving it would understate an fp8 deployment.
  • Not scoped by graph mode. vLLM measures the activation peak in an eager profile run and the capture separately (gpu_worker.py); a mode-scoped multiple would charge capture twice.
  • Not scoped by hardware, because the source states no per-part value; the scope lists every catalog part, under the same coverage test as the host set.

Engine. These are the vLLM figures. SGLang's table is about 1.3× higher with a further 15% overhead, and SGLang does not charge activations inside its static pool. A deployment states no engine identity and the consumer prices vLLM, so no SGLang row is registered.

Not registered: the MoE dispatch workspace. AISimulate adds tokens · h · num_experts · top_k / ep / 128 · 4 bytes for its DeepSeek-derived families and Kimi-K2.5 — 3,758,096,384 bytes for DeepSeek-V3 at 8,192 tokens and ep 1. That is a formula over catalog facts and the fp8 block size, not a learned magnitude, so it belongs to the consumer's composition; it is recorded here so it is not lost.

docs.title: 11.3 CUDA-graph capture — assumed, anchored on vLLM's own measurements
docs.text:
No dataset this project reads measures it. AISimulate takes it from the caller with a zero default; the FPM dataset records each run's cudagraph_mode and capture sizes in its resolved configs but no memory figure (all 417 of its JSON, text and TSV files under 3.5 MB at revision 68fa3add were read), and its SGLang raw evidence was collected with prefill capture off.

vLLM measures it on every start-up and logs it, and users paste those logs into issues. mine_vllm_cudagraph_memory.py collected 506 samples from 677 vLLM issues into registry/docs/vllm-cudagraph-capture-samples.csv, which is committed so the anchor is reproducible offline. The medians on catalog parts are 0.80 GiB for PIECEWISE (n = 18) and 1.08 GiB for FULL_AND_PIECEWISE (n = 22); the replaced constant was 0.50 GiB. The dimension is vLLM's profiler (gpu_model_runner.profile_cudagraph_memory): one first capture per mode, sized by the largest shape, plus at least 1 MiB per further graph, with PIECEWISE and FULL overlaid in one pool. So the cost is dominated by the largest captured shape, not proportional to the number of shapes.

FULL and FULL_DECODE_ONLY have too few samples (one and four logs, only one of them on a catalog part), so they are charged the FULL_AND_PIECEWISE figure as an upper bound — they capture a subset of its graphs into the same pool — with the direction declared. NONE is not_charged at zero.

Why this source is admissible here and nowhere else. §3's separation is about fitting: an uncontrolled sample cannot identify a per-primitive constant. These entries are not fitted and are not measured; they are assumed entries whose magnitude is oriented by the only public record of the quantity, in the pattern host_admission_per_request set. None of the samples is from InferenceX or FPM, and the single-sourcing tests (test_generated_from_aisimulate.py) still govern the primitive and collective sets, which this set is kept out of for exactly that reason.

docs.title: 11.4 What it changes on the issue's fixture
docs.text:
On deepseek-v3-h200-fp8-sglang-tp8 (tp 8, hidden_size 7168, 8,192 batched tokens, PIECEWISE), resolved through the cost model's own resolve.Load (kernel/internal/resolve):

term hardcoded registry activation scratch 469,762,048 (×4) 1,174,405,120 (MoE 8-rank ×10) CUDA-graph capture 536,870,912 858,783,744 collective buffers 411,041,792 411,041,792 (nccl_communicator_bytes_8rank) engine workspace not charged 3,758,096,384 total 1,417,674,752 6,202,327,040

The cost model reads every term of the set and refuses a scenario that does not list it (inference-sim/blis-latency-kernel#22).

docs.title: 12. Speculative acceptance profiles
docs.text: acceptance/inferencex-golden-al.yaml holds the acceptance lengths a simulator advances speculating requests by (inference-sim/blis-registry#44), in the contracts' acceptance format (blis-schemas#65). It is not a coefficient set: acceptance does not price a step, it sets how many tokens a step yields. The generated tables and the set's caveats are on the acceptance reference page.

docs.title: 12.1 One source, transcribed
docs.text: Every value comes from SemiAnalysis InferenceX's inferencex-e2e/infx/golden_al_distribution/*.yaml, vendored under validator/testdata/inferencex/ at the commit scripts/emit_acceptance_profiles.py cites. The emitter reads each acceptance length, and every provenance field a file's header states (the source Actions run, benchmark, category, sampling, image, TP and engine settings, including speculative-config: a=b | c=d lines), and types none of them. Every header is read, carried or not: a piece stating a value, as key: value or key=value with any spelling of key, that the emitter does not know how to transcribe fails the run, so a setting cannot be silently dropped. Only named prose lines are exempt. A header that states method: must state the curve's method; one that does not is checked against its "Measured on (..., vLLM )" line. An acceptance length is measured; the one file InferenceX marks provisional is transferred, with transferred_from naming the measured profile it repeats and transfer_rule stating why that carries over, and the emitter checks that the two values agree.

docs.title: 12.2 Model names: resolved, or refused
docs.text:
InferenceX keys a curve by the lower-cased basename of the Hugging Face repository it served (MODEL_KEY in its SPEED-Bench collectors). The emitter resolves that key to the catalog model whose source.repo has that basename, against the vendored copy of every catalog model.yaml. A key that resolves to none is not carried, and the set's caveats name it. A quantised checkpoint is a different catalog model, so InferenceX's qwen3.5-397b-a17b-nvfp4 does not become the catalog's bf16 qwen3.5-397b-a17b.

One alias is allowed, with its evidence in the emitter: glm-5.3-fp8, the provisional curve's key, is InferenceX's name for zai-org/GLM-5.3, the catalog's glm-5.3. The emitter fails if the catalog stops recording that repository for it.

docs.title: 12.3 Curves a key cannot tell apart
docs.text: A profile is keyed by model, method, K, thinking mode and category; it cannot state the drafter or the draft sampler. Where InferenceX publishes two curves that differ only in those, at most one can be carried. The emitter follows InferenceX's own resolver (curves.py, curve_name): MiniMax-M3's base EAGLE3 curve is carried and the GQA-drafter variant is not, and neither Kimi-K3 DSpark curve is carried, because the resolver itself refuses to choose between greedy and probabilistic draft sampling. Every file is classified in the emitter's CURVES table, and an unclassified file fails the run.

docs.title: 12.4 Hardware: stated, or read from the run
docs.text:
A measured profile must name the part it was measured on. Most headers state it ("B300, vLLM MTP"). The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash file states none, and its collecting job ran on InferenceX's b200-nscale cluster, launched through the B200 benchmark base, so its profiles say b200. blis-registry#44 describes the curve as measured on B300; the run contradicts that, and the run is what is recorded. The emitter's RUN_HARDWARE table holds each run's runner, read through the GitHub API, and is checked against every header that also states a part. Files that name no engine image say so in engine_image: their runs' logs have expired, so the image cannot be recovered.

The collectors are named <prefix>_fp4_b300_vllm.sh because speedbench-al.yml requires that name and labels every collection PRECISION: fp4; the fp4 is not what they serve. Each serves its checkpoint's own weights, and the DeepSeek-V4-Pro and GLM-5.2 collectors set --kv-cache-dtype fp8, which their profiles record as kv_cache_dtype. The emitter's COLLECTORS table holds what each collector serves, and a curve whose collector it has not read fails the run.

docs.title: 12.5 Gates
docs.text: emit_acceptance_profiles.py --check runs in every CI job (validator/test_acceptance_profiles.py), because its inputs are vendored. The rederive job also checks the vendored curves against InferenceX at its pinned commit (INFERENCEX_SHA in .github/workflows/rederive.yml), checks the catalog models against the repository's catalog/, and re-runs the emitter against the upstream checkout. Schema validation is validate-registry (validate/cmd/validate-registry), which reads acceptance/ (blis-schemas#74), in CI's registry job.

docs.title: Reproducing every coefficient from the original datasets
docs.text:
This guide takes a reader from two public datasets to the coefficient values this registry ships. It exists because a fitted constant whose fit cannot be re-run is not a measurement, it is a number someone wrote down. Two earlier sets in this registry — the per-GPU roofline-* MFU sets and trained-physics — were removed precisely because they could not be re-derived: trained-physics carried fifteen entries, eleven of them fitted: true, with no sources block on any entry and no fitter in scripts/; the five roofline-* sets carried two method: literature entries each, citing an issue number rather than a dataset. Both are recoverable from git history if ever needed.

For why the coefficients take the forms they do, and for the train/validate separation that governs which dataset may be used for what, read methodology.md first. This document is the mechanical companion: where the data comes from, and which command regenerates which file.

docs.title: AISimulate — per-operator sweeps and system descriptors
docs.text:
Repository https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate Docs https://ai-dynamo.org/aisimulate/ Licence Apache-2.0, with one MIT third-party file carved out in the LICENSE NOTICE and attributed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. GitHub's license API reports NOASSERTION because of that preamble; the text itself says "Except for the third-party material identified in that notice file, this codebase is licensed under the Apache License 2.0", and source files carry SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0. Provenance Successor to ai-dynamo/aiconfigurator; method described in arXiv:2601.06288. Fetch git clone https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate — the sweeps are checked into git as Parquet. Git LFS is needed only for retained legacy .txt assets, which no fit in this registry reads. pip install aisimulate also ships the tree inside the wheel. Pin Every committed value re-derives at 2f0f4cd8606d580567b253d02f3d699fe36db865 (2026-10-10), with the repository's own catalog/ at the same commit as the registry. The rederive workflow checks out AISimulate at AISIMULATE_SHA; bump it deliberately, with the diff the writers produce. A catalog change to a part's datasheet figure moves every rate fitted as a fraction of it, so the writers' --check runs on the pull request that makes it. Python pip install --require-hashes -r scripts/requirements-fit.txt, from registry/: the validator's dependencies plus numpy, pandas and pyarrow, which the fitters need to read Parquet.

The two trees the fits read are not at the repository root:

python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/<sku>.yaml          # system descriptors
python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/data/<sku>/<op>/<framework>/<version>/*.parquet

Export that second path once; every script below honours it. The fitters read the repository's catalog/ unless BLIS_CATALOG names another directory, and scripts/rederive.sh requires it. Run them from registry/:

export AISIMULATE_DATA=<aisimulate>/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/data
export BLIS_CATALOG=$PWD/../catalog

Dataset SKU directories are not catalog chip names. The sweeps use h200_sxm, h100_sxm, b200_sxm, b300_sxm, gb200, a100_sxm, l40s; the catalog calls the same parts h200, h100, b200, b300, gb200-nvl72, a100-sxm, l40s. The mapping lives in each fitter's SKUS table and is passed as sku:chip pairs. There is no gb200_nvl72 directory.

Framework lanes present in the data tree are vllm, sglang, trtllm and, for comm, nccl. Which lane is admissible for which operator is a methodology question, not a mechanical one — see the lane table in methodology.md.

docs.title: FPM — whole-forward-pass measurements
docs.text:
Dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/aisimulate-fpm-dataset ("AISimulate FPM Dataset"; FPM = Forward Pass Model) Licence Apache-2.0, same NVIDIA text and MIT carve-out as the code repository Pinning By commit SHA — the dataset has no tags and its history is actively rewritten. Cite a SHA, never main. Fetch huggingface_hub.snapshot_download(repo_id="nvidia/aisimulate-fpm-dataset", repo_type="dataset", revision=<sha>)

Layout is data/<org>--<model>/<system>/<framework>/<version>/<parallelism>/{manifest.json,fpm/,measurements/}. The per-leaf measurement Parquets under measurements/ are what this registry validates against; the three configs the HuggingFace datasets-server exposes (the catalog, fpm and measurements file-index configs, 326 rows in total) are file indexes, not measurements — a reader who stops at those will conclude the dataset is three hundred rows.

At the revision this registry validated against, the measurement Parquets hold 85,484 rows, every one backend: vllm, splitting by the KV axis into 12,522 pure decode (total_prefill_tokens == 0), 5,226 pure prefill (total_kv_read_tokens == 0) and 67,736 mixed. Derive these counts rather than quoting them: the dataset is rewritten, and the workload_kind column labels any row carrying prefill tokens as prefill, which is a coarser split than the one fitting needs.

FPM is used for validation and model selection. It may fit only a term that is itself a property of the whole forward pass, never a per-primitive constant, and no committed coefficient cites it. methodology.md §3 gives the argument, including why an earlier, stricter rule was relaxed.

docs.title: 2. What each dataset's units are
docs.text:
Two traps, both of which have produced wrong numbers in this project before:

  • latency in every AISimulate Parquet is MILLISECONDS. Reading it as seconds gives a 1000× error that happens to look plausible on some parts.
  • FPM's total_kv_read_tokens is summed OVER THE BATCH, while the kernel takes a per-request context length. Dividing by batch_size is required.

docs.title: 3. Regenerating each coefficient set
docs.text:
Run from the repository root with AISIMULATE_DATA and BLIS_CATALOG exported. Two sets are fully generated and are compared by diff; the rest are fitted per part, and each printed value should match the committed entry.

Entry counts quoted in this section were taken when each passage was written, and sets have grown since. The current count of every set, by method, is on the reference pages, which are generated from the committed files.

docs.title: cost-model-primitives.yaml — per-family writers
docs.text:
No single command regenerates this set; each family has an owner (table below), and emit_primitives.py owns only the vendor_spec descriptor entries. Those it reads from AISimulate's own systems/<sku>.yaml — the keys are mem_bw_empirical_scaling_factor, pcie_bw, misc.nccl_mem (the rank-count→bytes map) and misc.other_mem, several of which NVIDIA annotates in-file as "nonofficial correction based on observations". It takes the systems directory, not systems/data:

python scripts/emit_primitives.py \
    <aisimulate>/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems "$BLIS_CATALOG"

and its output is a reference to compare the descriptor entries against, not a file to commit whole (see the warning at the end of this section). Two descriptor keys are deliberately not emitted — mem_empirical_constant_latency and p2p_latency — because nothing in BLIS reads them and a reader would double-count the measured floors (methodology §1). a100_pcie is skipped and the a100_sxm descriptor is scoped to both A100 names (methodology §5).
